concepts.card: Chess ends in checkmate when the opposing king is attacked and no legal move can remove the threat. The king is never actually captured. A different ending, stalemate, occurs when a player has no legal move but their king is not attacked.

evidence.note: Articles 1.4 and 5.2.1 support the objective, prohibition of king capture and contrasting stalemate condition; no claim that every immobile king is stalemated.

imported_records.description: Exploring strategic play, tactics and positional thinking in chess.

concepts.label: Chess
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why checkmate ends play without capturing the king.
concepts.original_description: Exploring strategic play, tactics and positional thinking in chess.

relations.note: The laws distinguish checkmate from stalemate through whether the immobile side's king is attacked.

concepts.card: Go players place stones on grid intersections to surround space. Connected stones share liberties: empty neighboring intersections along the grid lines. When an opponent occupies every liberty, the whole connected string is captured, linking local fights over stones with the larger struggle for territory.

evidence.note: BGA introduction and capture paragraphs support intersections, orthogonal liberties and capture of a connected string; diagonal contact is not treated as connection.

imported_records.description: Exploring territorial strategy and pattern recognition in the game of Go.
board game for two players that originated in China more than 2,500 years ago
imported_records.subsection: Arts and recreation / Recreation: games and sports

concepts.label: Go
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect surrounding space with the capture of groups that lose every liberty.
concepts.original_description: Exploring territorial strategy and pattern recognition in the game of Go.

relations.note: The teaching guide explains Go capture through the shared liberties of connected stones.

concepts.card: Shogi is Japanese chess with a distinctive form of piece reuse. Captured pieces become reserves for their captor. Instead of moving a piece already on the board, a player can spend a turn returning a captured piece to play on their own side.

evidence.locator: Physical PDF pages 2, 4 and 13 (zero-based tool page indices 1, 3 and 12): introduction, Comparisons and Placing Captured Pieces
evidence.note: Captured pieces become the captor’s reserves and may be returned to play instead of moving a board piece; no unrestricted-drop or automatic-promotion claim is used.

imported_records.description: Exploring Japanese chess and its distinctive piece-reuse strategies.

concepts.label: Shogi
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain the piece-reuse feature of shogi through a directly supported broad-game overview, leaving the perpetual-check exception to its separate rule card.
concepts.original_description: Exploring Japanese chess and its distinctive piece-reuse strategies.

relations.note: The guide explicitly compares shogi with European chess and identifies returning captured pieces as a difference.

concepts.card: Backgammon combines a race with obstacles. Each player moves fifteen checkers according to dice rolls, aiming to gather them in the home board and remove them. Landing on a lone opposing checker sends it to the bar, where it must re-enter before other checkers move.

evidence.locator: Object of the Game and Movement
evidence.note: USBGF Object, Movement and Hitting sections support fifteen checkers, dice movement, bearing-off objective and priority of bar entry; a hit requires landing on a lone checker.

imported_records.description: Exploring strategic play involving movement, probability and dice.

concepts.label: Backgammon
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect dice-limited movement with the race to remove all fifteen checkers.
concepts.original_description: Exploring strategic play involving movement, probability and dice.

relations.note: The rules make re-entry of hit checkers a compulsory interruption of normal checker movement.

concepts.card: Othello changes the ownership of pieces already on the board. A player places a disc to bracket an uninterrupted line of opposing discs, then flips those discs to their color. The winner has more discs when neither player can make a legal move.

evidence.note: Official outflanking and ending rules support placement, flipping and the final majority; the game need not fill all sixty-four squares.

concepts.label: Othello
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how a placement changes ownership of intervening discs.

relations.note: A lack of outflanking moves determines both forced passes and the eventual end of the game.

concepts.card: In contract bridge, four players form two partnerships. Bidding establishes a contract specifying a number of tricks and a trump suit, or no trumps. During play, one partner's cards are exposed as dummy, and the declarer chooses cards from both partnership hands.

evidence.note: ACBL Basics, Auction and Play support partnerships, contract denomination and dummy control; bidding numbers count tricks above the initial six, so the card avoids equating the printed bid with total tricks.

imported_records.description: Exploring partnership bidding and trick-taking strategy.

concepts.label: Contract bridge
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how bidding fixes a partnership's trick-taking target before play.
concepts.original_description: Exploring partnership bidding and trick-taking strategy.

relations.note: ACBL's play explanation assigns the exposed partnership hand to declarer's decisions after the auction.

concepts.card: Senet used a thirty-square board in ancient Egypt. Its imagery became more than decoration: during the New Kingdom, the game's passage through marked hazards was associated with the deceased person's journey toward the afterlife. Surviving game boxes connect recreation with funerary belief.

evidence.locator: Senet; Why is this game important?
evidence.note: The Met's Senet and importance sections support thirty squares, New Kingdom association and funerary objects; avoid presenting reconstructed detailed rules as certain.

concepts.label: Senet
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect an Egyptian board race with New Kingdom beliefs about the afterlife.

relations.note: The museum documents double-sided game boxes carrying senet on one side and Twenty Squares on the other.

concepts.card: Twenty Squares spread across the ancient Near East and was later imported into Egypt. Surviving boards reveal adaptation rather than simple copying: special squares on Near Eastern examples display rosettes, while Egyptian examples use hieroglyphs. A shared game could acquire a different visual language.

evidence.note: The Met explicitly reports geographic spread, import into Egypt and contrasting markings; no claim that all surviving boards preserve markings or identical rules.

concepts.label: Twenty Squares
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how an imported ancient game acquired Egyptian markings and visual conventions.

relations.note: The museum describes Egyptian boxes accommodating both games, making their material comparison explicit.

concepts.card: Dick Fosbury's lasting influence came from the high-jump technique bearing his name. He won Olympic gold in 1968, but his legacy extended beyond that result: the Fosbury Flop transformed how the event was approached. Olympedia distinguishes this technical influence from his relatively brief competitive prominence.

evidence.note: Olympedia biography supports 1968 gold, technique and enduring influence; the card does not invent biomechanical details absent from this source.

concepts.label: Dick Fosbury
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine an athlete whose enduring influence came from a new jumping style.

relations.note: The biography identifies Fosbury's innovation and Olympic result specifically with the high-jump event.

concepts.card: James Naismith devised basketball at Springfield in 1891 to provide an engaging indoor winter activity. Avoiding the rough collisions of outdoor games shaped the design. Elevated peach baskets required players to toss the ball toward a goal rather than charge through it.

evidence.locator: A New Game; The Birth of Basketball
evidence.note: Springfield's account supports the winter brief, concern about roughness, elevated baskets and tossing; it does not establish that every modern rule originated unchanged in 1891.

concepts.label: James Naismith
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how indoor space and injury constraints shaped basketball's original design.

relations.note: The college's historical account identifies Naismith as basketball's inventor and explains the game's design constraints.

concepts.card: An en passant capture answers a pawn's two-square first advance. An opposing pawn beside its destination may capture it as though it had moved only one square. The opportunity exists only on the immediately following move; waiting forfeits this particular capture.

evidence.note: FIDE 3.7.3.1–2 supports neighboring same-rank pawns, the two-square advance and immediate-next-move limit; no other capture window is implied.

concepts.label: En passant
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand the pawn capture available only immediately after a neighboring two-square advance.

relations.note: FIDE defines en passant as a special pawn capture within the chess movement rules.

concepts.card: Castling moves a king and rook in one turn, but permission depends on more than empty squares. Moving the king or the relevant rook permanently loses that castling right. Pieces between them or attacks on the king's starting, crossing or destination square can temporarily prevent it.

evidence.note: FIDE 3.8.2 distinguishes forfeited rights from temporary obstruction; the attacked-square restriction concerns the king's route, not every square the rook crosses.

concepts.label: Castling
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish permanent loss of castling rights from temporary obstacles.

relations.note: FIDE explicitly defines castling as a king-and-rook move within the chess movement rules.

concepts.card: Stalemate is a drawn chess position in which the player to move has no legal move and their king is not in check. The distinction from checkmate is crucial: immobilizing the opponent does not win if no attack on the king accompanies that immobilization.

evidence.note: FIDE 5.2.1 supports side-to-move, absence of any legal move, no check and immediate draw; immobility of one piece alone is insufficient.

concepts.label: Stalemate
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish having no legal move from being checkmated.

relations.note: The laws define stalemate as one of chess's game-ending draw conditions.

concepts.card: A dead position ends a chess game because neither player could checkmate through any possible sequence of legal moves. This is stronger than saying that checkmate seems unlikely or cannot be forced: even cooperative play by the opponent would not make mate possible.

evidence.note: FIDE 5.2.2 quantifies over any legal sequence; the cooperative-play explanation unpacks that condition rather than adding a material-count rule.

concepts.label: Dead position in chess
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize a draw where neither side can ever deliver legal checkmate.

relations.note: Both end the game as a draw, but stalemate concerns present legal moves while dead position concerns impossibility of future mate.

concepts.card: In over-the-board chess, a player whose turn it is normally must move the first deliberately touched own piece that has a legal move. Announcing an intention to adjust a piece before touching it is different. Clearly accidental contact does not count as deliberate selection.

evidence.note: FIDE 4.2–4.5 restricts binding touch to the player having the move, prioritizes the first legally movable own piece, and distinguishes announced adjustment and clearly accidental contact.

concepts.label: Touch-move rule
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how deliberate touching commits a player when a legal move exists.

relations.note: FIDE's Act of Moving the Pieces regulates how a player's physical selection becomes binding.

concepts.card: Under FIDE rules, threefold repetition permits a draw claim rather than automatically ending play. The player to move may claim when the position has appeared for the third time, or record an intended move producing it and declare that intention to the arbiter before moving.

evidence.note: FIDE 9.2.1–2 supports current-position claims and intended-move claims recorded and declared to the arbiter before execution; 9.6.1 separately supplies the automatic fivefold contrast.

concepts.label: Threefold repetition
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain the claimable three-occurrence draw procedure, including the timing of a claim before a qualifying intended move.

relations.note: The rules distinguish a player's threefold claim from the automatic fivefold repetition draw.

concepts.card: A pawn reaching its final rank need not become a queen. Underpromotion chooses a rook, bishop or knight instead. The new piece takes effect immediately, and the available choices do not depend on which pieces were captured earlier in the game.

evidence.note: FIDE 3.7.3.3–5 support all alternatives, immediate effect and independence from captured pieces; no unsupported tactical claim explains why a particular choice wins.

concepts.label: Underpromotion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize that promotion may choose a rook, bishop or knight instead of queen.

relations.note: FIDE's pawn-promotion rule explicitly permits the three non-queen choices described here.

concepts.card: A liberty is an empty intersection directly beside a Go stone along a horizontal or vertical line. Connected stones share their liberties as one string. Surrounding every liberty captures the entire string, so adding a connection can change the survival prospects of several stones at once.

evidence.note: BGA capture section supports orthogonal adjacency and whole-string treatment; the connection consequence follows directly from sharing the resulting string's liberties.

concepts.label: Liberties in Go
concepts.learning_takeaway: Count shared adjacent empty points for an entire connected string.

relations.note: The Go guide uses liberties to define when individual stones and connected strings are captured.

concepts.card: An eye is an internal space in a connected Go group. Two genuine, separate eyes can keep a group safe: an opponent cannot fill both in one move, and occupying the first would be self-capture rather than capturing the surrounding stones.

evidence.locator: Life and death and the concept of eyes
evidence.note: BGA Life and death and self-capture examples support two-eye safety; genuine eyes prevents confusing superficial holes with the protected spaces in the rule explanation.

concepts.label: Eyes in Go
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why two separate internal spaces protect a group from capture.

relations.note: The guide explains eye-based survival through internal liberties and the prohibition on noncapturing self-capture.

concepts.card: A ko capture can create an opportunity for immediate recapture that would restore the previous position. The basic ko rule forbids that immediate reply. The player must first play elsewhere, giving the opponent an opportunity to respond or end the local cycle.

evidence.note: BGA ko diagrams and explanatory paragraph support immediate-recapture restriction and intervening play; this does not claim that a single intervening move overrides every superko rule.
Superko forbids longer repeating positions; the comparison is editorial.

concepts.label: Ko rule
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why immediate recapture must wait for a play elsewhere.

relations.note: Immediate ko and situational superko both limit repetition, but the latter also addresses longer cycles such as triple ko.

concepts.card: Seki is mutual survival in Go without each group having two independent eyes. Neighboring groups share a shortage of liberties, and either player's attempt to capture can allow the opponent to capture first. Leaving the position alone therefore preserves both sides' stones.

evidence.locator: Seki: a kind of local stalemate
evidence.note: BGA's seki examples support mutual stand-off and shortage of liberties; no universal territory-scoring rule is added because rulesets differ.

concepts.label: Seki
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize mutual survival when either attack would allow the opponent to capture.

relations.note: The guide introduces seki as an exception to the simple expectation that a group lacking two eyes will die.

concepts.card: Komi compensates the player using White stones for Black's first move in Go. It adds points to White's final score rather than adding stones to the board. The British Go Association's cited default uses seven-and-a-half points; other rules or agreements can use different values.

evidence.note: BGA Default Rules gives 7½ and contrasts traditional Japanese values; How to Play explains compensation rather than placement of stones.
The guide explains compensation to White for Black moving first.

concepts.label: Komi
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand points compensating White for playing second.

relations.note: The tournament rules identify komi as a score adjustment within Go, separately from handicap-stone placement.

concepts.card: Under the British Go Association's AGA-style rule, a player cannot make a play that recreates a board position previously created by that player. This reaches beyond immediate ko recapture, preventing longer repeating cycles such as triple ko from continuing indefinitely.

evidence.note: The precise BGA same-player formulation and triple-ko motivation are retained; this is not asserted to describe every international superko variant.

concepts.label: Situational superko
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare a whole-game repetition ban with the immediate ko restriction.

relations.note: BGA describes its superko restriction as preventing triple ko and other repeated positions beyond the basic local cycle.

concepts.card: Territory scoring counts enclosed empty points and captured stones; area scoring counts enclosed points and stones still occupying the board. That difference changes whether filling your own territory costs a point. AGA rules use pass stones to permit territory-style counting within an area-scoring framework.

evidence.note: BGA comparison explicitly supports both definitions, defensive-fill consequence and pass-stone accommodation; the card avoids claiming universal exact equality of final counts.

concepts.label: Area and territory scoring in Go
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare counting occupied points with counting territory plus prisoners.

relations.note: The comparison identifies these as alternative Go scoring systems and explains their practical counting differences.

concepts.card: When doubling is allowed in backgammon, a player offers it at the start of their own turn, before rolling. The opponent can decline and lose at the old value, or accept. Acceptance gives that player the cube and the exclusive right to offer the next redouble.

evidence.note: USBGF Doubling supports own-turn timing, before rolling, refusal cost and ownership. When allowed preserves format exceptions such as the separately discussed Crawford game; this is descriptive scoring, not advice to gamble.

concepts.label: Doubling cube
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how accepting a double transfers the right to offer the next redouble.

relations.note: The federation presents the cube as the game's mechanism for offering and accepting increased stakes.

concepts.card: A backgammon loser who has not removed any checkers suffers a gammon, worth twice the doubling cube's value under standard scoring. If that loser also has a checker on the bar or in the winner's home board, the loss is instead a triple-value backgammon.

evidence.note: USBGF Gammons and Backgammons supports the two scoring conditions; standard scoring qualification leaves room for the separately selected optional Jacoby rule.

concepts.label: Gammon
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why losing before bearing off any checker doubles the game's value.

relations.note: USBGF explicitly describes Jacoby as an optional rule changing when gammon and backgammon multipliers count.

concepts.card: Bearing off removes checkers from a backgammon board, but only after all your active checkers reach your home board. A roll normally removes a checker from its matching point. An oversized roll can remove the highest remaining checker when no checker occupies a higher point.

evidence.note: USBGF Bearing Off supplies prerequisites and oversized-roll rule; wording avoids requiring removal when another legal move is possible.

concepts.label: Bearing off in backgammon
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore the conditions for removing checkers and using an oversized die roll.

relations.note: Bearing off is explicitly the final removal process that completes backgammon's race.

concepts.card: A lone backgammon checker hit by an opponent goes to the bar. Its owner must bring barred checkers back into the opponent's home board before moving other pieces. If the dice offer no open entry point, the player's turn is lost.

evidence.note: USBGF Hitting and Entering supports hit, priority and failed entry; the chosen example concerns no available entry, not partial entry with several checkers.

concepts.label: Bar entry in backgammon
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why a hit checker must return before other pieces can move.

relations.note: The rules make bar entry a compulsory recovery step after a checker is hit.

concepts.card: The optional Jacoby rule makes a gammon or backgammon count as a single game unless a double has been offered. It encourages use of the cube rather than waiting for a multiple-value win. The cited standard match-play rules do not use it.

evidence.locator: Optional Rules: Jacoby Rule; FAQ on match play
evidence.note: USBGF Optional Rules gives the condition and incentive; its match-play FAQ explicitly excludes Jacoby. The card preserves that format boundary instead of treating the optional convention as universal.

concepts.label: Jacoby rule
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how an optional scoring rule encourages use of the doubling cube.

relations.note: The source explains Jacoby's purpose through whether players use the doubling cube during the game.

concepts.card: Passing in Othello is compulsory when you cannot legally outflank an opposing disc, but forbidden when a legal move is available. Your opponent may therefore move twice in succession. If neither player can move, the game ends even when some squares remain empty.

evidence.note: World Othello rules 2 and 8 support mandatory pass, prohibition of voluntary pass and early ending; no claim that every pass immediately ends play.

concepts.label: Forced passing in Othello
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish being unable to move from choosing to pass strategically.

relations.note: The official game rules define passing entirely through legal outflanking moves.

concepts.card: Repeated checking is not a safe route to a draw in shogi. Under the Japan Shogi Association's cited explanation, if continuous checks produce the same position four times, the player giving those checks loses. Ordinary repetition without continuous checking is treated differently.

evidence.locator: 連続王手の千日手というのは反則なのですか
evidence.note: The official Japanese FAQ supports the fourth-occurrence loss and distinguishes ordinary repetition; the broad Shogi card instead explains piece reuse.

concepts.label: Perpetual check in shogi
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare ordinary repetition with repeated checks that make the checking player lose.

relations.note: The Japan Shogi Association identifies this as shogi's special treatment of repetition by continuous check.

concepts.card: Under the cited professional shogi impasse procedure, both kings have entered enemy territory and neither mating prospects nor further captures remain. Rooks and bishops count five points; other nonking pieces count one. Both players having at least twenty-four points leads to a draw and replay.

evidence.locator: 持将棋の規定はどうなっていますか
evidence.note: The Japan Shogi Association FAQ specifies professional play, both kings entering enemy territory, no mating prospect or further captures, and at least 24 points each. Amateur 27-point and declaration procedures are not generalized.

concepts.label: Shogi impasse
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore material counting when neither advanced king can plausibly be mated.

relations.note: The official FAQ describes material-count adjudication as a shogi procedure and distinguishes professional from amateur variants.

concepts.card: Duplicate bridge compares results from players holding the same deal of cards. A weak hand is therefore judged against what others achieved with that weak hand, rather than against opponents lucky enough to receive stronger cards. The format reduces the influence of the deal's initial luck.

evidence.note: ACBL Duplicate Bridge supports identical deals and comparison against the field; reduces rather than eliminates chance, without claiming every duplicate scoring system is identical.

concepts.label: Duplicate bridge
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand comparison against other players holding the same cards.

relations.note: ACBL presents duplicate as a bridge format in which the same deals are played at multiple tables.

concepts.card: Vulnerability changes bridge's rewards and risks: successful contracts can earn higher bonuses, while failed contracts can incur greater penalties. In duplicate bridge, the board determines which partnership is vulnerable. This differs from rubber bridge, where winning a game changes a partnership's vulnerability.

evidence.note: ACBL vulnerability definition supports premiums, undertrick penalties and the two different assignment methods; does not conflate vulnerable status with the strength of a hand.

concepts.label: Vulnerability in bridge
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how increased bonuses and penalties change a contract's stakes.

relations.note: ACBL describes vulnerability as a scoring status affecting bridge bonuses and penalties, then distinguishes its assignment in duplicate and rubber formats.

concepts.card: After contract bridge's opening lead, the declarer's partner lays their hand face up as dummy. The declarer chooses which cards to play from both partnership hands. This creates a distinctive information pattern: defenders can see one opposing hand, but not the declarer's concealed cards.

evidence.note: ACBL Play supports timing, exposed dummy and declarer's control; the information consequence is directly entailed, without claiming defenders see each other's hands.

concepts.label: Dummy in bridge
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why one partnership hand becomes visible and is played by declarer's instructions.

relations.note: The play instructions define dummy as a specific role within the declaring partnership.

concepts.card: An offside position is judged when a teammate plays or touches the ball, but position alone is not an offence. Penalization requires the specified involvement in active play. A player receiving the ball directly from a goal kick, throw-in or corner kick commits no offside offence.

evidence.note: IFAB Law 11.1–11.3 fixes the position assessment at the teammate play/touch and separately requires active involvement. Direct goal-kick, throw-in and corner-kick receipt are the stated exceptions; no exhaustive geometry or contact-point nuance is asserted.

concepts.label: Offside in association football
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish occupying an offside position from committing an offside offence.

relations.note: IFAB identifies offside as Law 11 within association football's Laws of the Game.

concepts.card: A spinning baseball can experience a sideways aerodynamic force that bends its path. NASA's simplified curveball model links the curvature to spin, speed and air density. It treats the path as a circular arc when drag and the resulting changes in the force are neglected.

evidence.note: NASA Aerodynamic Force gives the spinning-ball force and explicitly states the approximation; retain model qualification rather than declaring every real pitch a circular arc.

concepts.label: Curveball aerodynamics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect spin-generated sideways force with a curved pitch trajectory.

relations.note: NASA explicitly explains the curveball through aerodynamic force acting on a spinning baseball.

concepts.card: A curveball's behavior depends partly on the air around it. In NASA's simplified model, lower air density weakens the aerodynamic deflection of a spinning pitch, all else equal. High-altitude conditions can therefore make a curveball travel along a straighter path.

evidence.note: NASA's equation discussion directly links lower density with larger curvature radius; all-else-equal and simplified-model language avoid unsupported prediction of every pitch or game statistic.

concepts.label: Altitude effects on baseball pitches
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore why thinner air weakens a spinning baseball's curvature, other factors equal.

relations.note: The source derives the altitude effect as a particular prediction of its curveball trajectory model.

concepts.card: A baseball's seams make its surface aerodynamically uneven. As their orientation changes during flight, the effective location and direction of aerodynamic forces can vary. NASA connects these unsteady forces with the knuckleball's erratic motion, rather than explaining it solely through a steady spin-generated curve.

evidence.locator: Lift: stitches and center of pressure
evidence.note: NASA Forces on a Baseball, Lift, supports seam-dependent pressure changes and erratic motion; contrast with its separate simplified curveball model is labeled editorial in the relationship.
Steady spinning-ball trajectory is a comparison premise, not the knuckleball explanation itself.

concepts.label: Knuckleball aerodynamics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand erratic flight from seam-dependent forces varying during the pitch.

relations.note: Contrasting seam-sensitive, time-varying forces with a regular spinning-ball model separates two different explanations of curved baseball flight.

concepts.card: Topspin helps a tennis ball dip into the court after clearing the net, allowing a faster shot to remain in play. Producing it depends on the racket's upward motion relative to the incoming ball, its tilt, and the ball's existing motion and spin.

evidence.note: Cross's Ball Spin discussion supports dipping trajectory and multiple determinants; this is a tennis example of the registered generic topspin identity, not a novel application ID.

imported_records.description: property of a rotating ball
imported_records.hook: Explore how a spinning ball's motion changes a shot's trajectory and bounce.

concepts.label: Topspin
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how topspin permits a faster shot to dip back into court.
concepts.original_description: property of a rotating ball

relations.note: Cross explicitly explains topspin production and its effect on shot trajectories in tennis.

concepts.card: Physicist Rod Cross distinguishes a tennis racket's vibration-node sweet spot from its center of percussion and point of fastest rebound. An impact at the vibration node removes that component of handle motion, but rotation and translation can still transmit forces to the hand.

evidence.note: Cross sections 1 and 3 expressly separate the vibration node, center of percussion and maximum rebound, with rotation/translation/vibration components. Attribution avoids treating one terminology choice as the only sense of sweet spot.

concepts.label: Tennis racket sweet spot
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a low-vibration impact location from the point of maximum rebound speed.

relations.note: The source directly compares a vibration-node sweet spot with the separate center-of-percussion concept.

concepts.card: An impact makes a tennis racket both recoil and rotate. At a particular supporting point, those motions can cancel. The corresponding impact location is its center of percussion. Adding the hand's mass shifts this relationship, so a freely suspended racket does not reproduce every playing condition.

evidence.note: Cross's Centre of percussion section defines conjugate supporting and impact points and the hand-mass shift; this is not a universal fixed spot on every racket.

concepts.label: Center of percussion in a tennis racket
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how recoil and rotation can cancel motion at a particular supporting point.

relations.note: Cross distinguishes cancellation of recoil and rotation from the separate vibration-node explanation of the sweet spot.

concepts.card: A ball dropped onto a suitably supported racket can stop almost dead after striking a particular location. Cross explains this through matching effective masses: the ball transfers its energy to the racket instead of rebounding strongly. The same location behaves differently when the racket is moving.

evidence.note: Cross's Dead spot experiment supplies the support condition, effective-mass explanation and moving-racket contrast; avoid presenting this as an invariant no-rebound point in all strokes.

concepts.label: Tennis racket dead spot
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand an impact location where a stationary racket can absorb nearly all the ball's energy.

relations.note: Low rebound at a dead spot and reduced handle vibration at a sweet spot answer different questions about an impact.

concepts.card: A cyclist riding in another rider's wake can encounter less aerodynamic resistance and use less energy to maintain speed. The leading rider can also gain a smaller benefit. Road-racing groups exploit this shared airflow, although position and spacing affect how much shelter each rider receives.

evidence.note: Exploratorium explains follower and leader advantages and spacing dependence; avoid exporting its numerical savings to all speeds, terrains or formations.

concepts.label: Drafting in cycling
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect riding in another cyclist's wake with reduced aerodynamic effort.

relations.note: The museum's Aerodynamics and Drafting explanation explicitly applies wake airflow to road cycling.

concepts.card: World Curling's 2024 report describes sweepers using pressure, brush angle and technique to influence a stone's distance and curl. Athletes test methods on different ice surfaces and disagree about some effects. The account documents evolving practice rather than establishing that every reported technique works equally well.

evidence.note: The 12 January 2024 governing-body report quotes athletes about pressure, angle, surface testing and disputed knifing effects. Claims are attributed to this historical practitioner account, not certified as universal controlled findings or current equipment legality.

concepts.label: Sweeping in curling
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore altering stone travel through work on the ice rather than touching the stone.

relations.note: The governing body's report describes sweeping as a technique within curling that changes the stone's travel through surface work.

concepts.card: Rhythmic augmentation stretches a musical idea in time while preserving its relative durations. A motive in quarter notes might return in half notes, with every value doubled. This differs from simply adding notes at the end: the existing pattern itself occupies more time.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 11.2.3 defines usual proportional doubling; the contrast with extension is supported by 11.2.6. Preserve the registered rhythmic-augmentation control.

concepts.label: Rhythmic augmentation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize a motive whose durations expand proportionally while its pitch pattern remains recognizable.

relations.note: The text explicitly presents diminution as the opposite temporal transformation to augmentation.

concepts.card: Musical diminution shortens the rhythmic values of a motive or phrase, commonly by halving every duration. The pitch sequence can remain recognizable while the idea unfolds faster. Some uses of the term are less exact, referring more generally to a passage rewritten with shorter note values.

evidence.note: Section 11.2.3 supports both exact halving and the broader usage; commonly prevents treating halving as an exceptionless definition.

concepts.label: Musical diminution
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish proportional rhythmic shortening from changing only some durations.

relations.note: The textbook defines diminution in direct contrast with augmentation's usual doubling of durations.

concepts.card: A melodic retrograde presents notes in the reverse order. It differs from melodic inversion, which reverses the direction of intervals rather than the sequence itself. Reading a tune backward and turning its upward leaps into downward leaps are therefore two distinct ways to transform musical material.

evidence.note: Sections 11.2.7 and 11.2.1 support order reversal versus interval-direction reversal; no claim that retrograde necessarily reverses every performance parameter.

concepts.label: Melodic retrograde
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hear how reversing note order differs from inverting intervals.

relations.note: Comparing the two definitions separates reversal of event order from reversal of melodic direction.

concepts.card: Melodic inversion turns an idea's interval directions upside down. A rising movement becomes a falling one. Real inversion preserves the precise sizes and qualities of intervals, while tonal inversion adjusts them to fit the scale or key, allowing the transformed melody to remain within its tonal setting.

evidence.note: Section 11.2.1 explicitly distinguishes real and tonal inversion; the tonal-setting consequence restates its scale/key qualification rather than claiming every interval is unchanged.

concepts.label: Melodic inversion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish interval-preserving real inversion from key-preserving tonal inversion.

relations.note: Inversion changes interval direction; retrograde changes note order, so their labels should not be treated as aliases.

concepts.card: An appoggiatura is a non-chord tone approached by a leap and left by a step. It is usually accented, placing the dissonance on a strong moment before resolution. The resolving step can go upward or downward; the expressive effect does not require one fixed direction.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 10.4 supports leap approach, step departure, usual accent and either resolution direction; maintain its analytical sense rather than every historical ornamental use of the term.
The prepared same-note approach of a suspension supports the editorial contrast.

concepts.label: Appoggiatura
concepts.learning_takeaway: Follow an expressive non-chord note approached by leap and resolved by step.

relations.note: Both can create accented non-chord tension, but an appoggiatura arrives by leap whereas a suspension is prepared by the same note.

concepts.card: A pedal point holds one note while surrounding harmonies change. It begins as a chord tone but can become a non-chord tone against later chords. Often heard in the bass, it can also appear higher up, creating continuity while its harmonic meaning shifts.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 10.8 supports changing harmonic status, frequent bass placement and upper-voice pedals; the card does not restrict the device to a literal organ pedal.

concepts.label: Pedal point
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hear a held note change harmonic status while surrounding chords move.

relations.note: Both can sustain a note across a harmonic change, but the pedal persists across harmonies while a suspension has a prepared stepwise resolution.

concepts.card: A suspension carries a prepared note into a moment where it becomes an accented non-chord tone, then resolves downward by step. Its three stages are preparation, suspension and resolution. Labels such as 4–3 describe the changing interval above the bass rather than the note's absolute pitch.

evidence.note: Section 10.9 supports preparation, accent, downward step and numbered intervals; bass suspensions have a special reference voice, so the card uses the ordinary 4–3 example.

concepts.label: Suspension in tonal music
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace preparation, accented dissonance and downward stepwise resolution.

relations.note: A suspension is approached by the same note, whereas an appoggiatura is approached by leap; their accented tension does not make them identical.

concepts.card: A cadential six-four contains the notes of a tonic triad with its fifth in the bass, yet commonly functions as part of a dominant arrival. Before the following dominant chord, its pitch content and its harmonic role therefore point in different analytical directions.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 16.3 explicitly identifies I6/4 preceding V and its dominant function; commonly avoids asserting that every second-inversion tonic is a cadential six-four.

concepts.label: Cadential six-four chord
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why an inverted tonic sonority can perform a dominant function.

relations.note: This sonority illustrates how harmonic function can differ from a chord's apparent tonic pitch content.

concepts.card: Additive minimalism develops music by expanding repeated material in small steps. In Glass's examples, repetitions may be added or chords given extra subdivisions. The listener can follow a process of gradual growth rather than waiting for an entirely new theme to replace the existing pattern.

evidence.locator: 35.1 Two Pages and Einstein on the Beach examples
evidence.note: Section 35.1 supplies Two Pages, Music in Fifths and lengthened chords in Einstein on the Beach; this describes the demonstrated processes rather than all minimalist composition.

concepts.label: Additive minimalism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Track growth by gradually extending repeated musical patterns.

relations.note: The textbook uses Glass's Two Pages as an explicit example of additive process combined with subtraction within repetitions.

concepts.card: Phase shifting changes the alignment of repeated musical patterns. One part can retain its timing while another gradually runs ahead, or a performer can jump directly to the next rotation. Reich's Piano Phase and Clapping Music demonstrate these different ways of reorganizing the same recurring material.

evidence.note: Section 35.2 explicitly contrasts gradual speeding in Piano Phase with discrete rotations in Clapping Music; no claim that both works require continuous tempo drift.

concepts.label: Musical phase shifting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare gradual desynchronization with discrete shifts of a repeated pattern.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly identifies Piano Phase as a live-performance application of Reich's phase-shifting process.

concepts.card: A fugue's answer is a subject entry associated with the dominant key. In a tonal answer, some intervals are changed to accommodate the movement between tonic and dominant. A real answer instead preserves the intervals, making tonal function and literal transposition different possible priorities.

evidence.note: Fugue Analysis defines answer, tonal modification and real preservation; associated with dominant leaves room for an answer beginning in tonic before moving there.

concepts.label: Tonal answer in fugue
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why a fugue answer alters intervals to navigate tonic and dominant.

relations.note: The answer is explicitly defined as a structural element of a fugue's subject-entry process.

concepts.card: A countersubject is recurring counterpoint that accompanies a fugue's subject. Its identity matters: the composer brings back recognizable accompanying material when the subject returns, rather than inventing completely different counterpoint each time. The same countersubject can appear in different voices as the texture changes.

evidence.note: Fugue Analysis defines consistent accompaniment and identifies one countersubject in alto and soprano; no requirement that every fugue have one is imposed.

concepts.label: Countersubject
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify recurring counterpoint accompanying successive subject entries.

relations.note: The source defines countersubject specifically within its fugue analysis and contrasts it with nonrecurring accompaniment.

concepts.card: Pitch is a sound's perceived highness or lowness. On a piano, moving right produces higher notes. For periodic musical tones, doubling the vibration frequency raises pitch by an octave, showing why musical intervals depend on frequency ratios rather than equal additions of hertz.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 1.1 supports keyboard direction; UNSW's pitch discussion supplies periodic-tone frequency and octave ratio. Keep this auditory meaning separate from material pitch.

evidence.locator: Pitch, frequency, harmonics and missing fundamental
evidence.note: Frequency ratios, including doubling for an octave, support the quantitative explanation.

concepts.label: Pitch (music)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Relate perceived high and low notes to their ordering on a keyboard.

relations.note: The UNSW pitch discussion explicitly uses a missing fundamental to show that perceived pitch can persist when the lowest-frequency component is absent.

concepts.card: Real instrument strings are not perfectly flexible. Their bending stiffness shifts higher vibration modes farther from exact whole-number multiples of the fundamental. This inharmonicity is especially relevant to plucked or struck strings; periodic bowing can instead draw the vibration into a harmonic pattern.

evidence.note: UNSW harmonics discussion supports stiffness and stronger high-mode shifts, with the bowed versus plucked/struck qualification; not every real string is claimed equally inharmonic.

concepts.label: Inharmonicity of musical strings
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why stiff strings have stretched modal frequencies rather than exact harmonic multiples.

relations.note: The article explicitly contrasts inharmonic string resonances with harmonic motion enforced by bow-driven mode locking.

concepts.card: A bow alternately sticks to and slips against a string, sustaining a nearly periodic motion. That nonlinear drive can pull the string's slightly mismatched resonances into harmonic frequency ratios. The resulting steady note can therefore be more harmonically regular than the freely vibrating string's natural modes.

evidence.note: UNSW explicitly attributes harmonic locking to periodic stick-slip drive; can and steady note preserve its operating-condition qualification.

concepts.label: Mode locking in bowed strings
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how periodic bowing can enforce harmonic motion despite inharmonic string resonances.

relations.note: The source explains mode locking as the reason bowed motion can be harmonic despite slightly inharmonic natural resonances.

concepts.card: Lightly touching a string at a suitable point suppresses vibrations incompatible with a node there, bringing out a higher mode. Natural harmonics use an open string. Artificial harmonics combine stopping the string with a second light touch, giving the player access to different starting pitches.

evidence.note: UNSW Strings explains touch-created nodes and open versus stopped strings; the second touch is not pressed firmly against the fingerboard.

imported_records.description: string instrument technique

concepts.label: String harmonic
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare lightly touching an open string with touching a separately stopped string.
concepts.original_description: string instrument technique

relations.note: The source gives a violin touch-fourth example, linking string-harmonic production with an actual performance technique on that instrument.

concepts.card: An untouched guitar string can vibrate when another string is plucked. Harmonic components pass through the bridge and excite a compatible resonance in the second string. The apparent response at a distance therefore involves transferred mechanical energy and matched frequencies, not a second deliberate pluck.

evidence.locator: Exercise for guitarists before Harmonic tuning on guitars
evidence.note: UNSW's guitar exercise explicitly links the low E string, bridge and B or high E strings; compatible resonance avoids asserting every string responds equally to every note.

imported_records.description: harmonic phenomenon in music

concepts.label: Sympathetic resonance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how shared harmonics transfer vibration through a guitar bridge.
concepts.original_description: harmonic phenomenon in music

relations.note: Shared harmonic frequencies help explain which unplayed strings respond, connecting resonance transfer with the harmonic modes used by performers.

concepts.card: In Steve Reich's Clapping Music, rhythmic alignment changes through discrete rotations of a repeated pattern. One performer maintains the original pattern while the other moves to the next alignment on a measure's downbeat. Unlike Piano Phase, the transition does not require gradually speeding up.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 35.2 directly names the work and discrete-rotation contrast; do not describe its shifting as continuous tape-style drift.

concepts.label: Clapping Music
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hear how discrete rhythmic rotations create changing alignments without a gradual tempo drift.

relations.note: The textbook identifies Clapping Music as a live-performance phase-shifting example using discrete rotations.

concepts.card: Steve Reich's Piano Phase makes a repeating twelve-note pattern change through alignment rather than replacement. A second pianist gradually increases speed relative to the other part, causing the patterns to slip out of phase. The process lets different combinations emerge from recurring material.

evidence.note: Section 35.2 supports the twelve-note pattern and second pianist's gradual speed change; emergent combinations follow from changing alignment, without an unsupported claim about exact complete formal design.

concepts.label: Piano Phase
concepts.learning_takeaway: Follow two repeated patterns as one pianist gradually changes their alignment.

relations.note: The source explicitly presents the work as Reich's application of phase shifting to live pianists.

concepts.card: At the opening of Philip Glass's Two Pages, growth comes from adding repetitions whose final notes are progressively removed. A motive can therefore expand while newly added units become shorter. The cited analysis illustrates how repetition and subtraction can cooperate within an additive process.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 35.1 explicitly limits its Two Pages demonstration to the opening and labels the notation a transcription/analysis. The card does not assert that every section of the entire work follows the displayed process.

concepts.label: Two Pages
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore Glass's additive process through repetitions that successively omit final notes.

relations.note: The textbook analyzes the opening of Glass's Two Pages as an example of additive process, with shortening repetitions inside the expanding unit.

concepts.card: The Train scene in Philip Glass's Einstein on the Beach provides a concrete example of additive process. A five-chord progression gradually lengthens as each chord receives more subdivisions. Musical change comes from stretching the allotted duration of recurring harmonies rather than continuously introducing new chords.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 35.1 describes the named scene, five chords and added subdivisions; the claim is limited to that example, not the entire opera.

concepts.label: Einstein on the Beach
concepts.learning_takeaway: Observe a five-chord progression expanding through added subdivisions.

relations.note: The source explicitly recommends the Train scene as an example of additive growth in chord duration.

concepts.card: Bach's C-minor fugue from the first Well-Tempered Clavier offers a compact lesson in contrapuntal development. Its opening exposition introduces the subject in every voice. Episodes then work with smaller fragments of subjects and countersubjects, allowing recognizable material to generate passages without a complete subject statement.

evidence.note: The detailed analysis identifies first exposition, all-voice entries and fragmented material in episodes; no unsupported numerical count of voices or episodes is added.

concepts.label: Bach's Fugue in C minor, BWV 847
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace full subject entries alternating with development through fragmented motives.

relations.note: The source explicitly analyzes BWV 847 as a fugue with expositions and episodes.

concepts.card: Bach's C-major Invention shows how a short idea can sustain development. The opening notes return with their melodic direction inverted, and fragments also appear in rhythmic augmentation. These transformations preserve recognizable material while changing its contour or the amount of time it occupies.

evidence.note: Section 11.2 identifies the first seven notes inverted later and an augmented fragment; the wording does not claim every occurrence transforms the whole theme.

concepts.label: Bach's Invention in C major, BWV 772
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize inversion and rhythmic augmentation within one tightly developed keyboard work.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly labels the invention's returning opening notes as melodic inversion.

concepts.card: Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings provides a textbook example of a 4–3 suspension. A prepared note becomes dissonant against the bass before resolving downward by step. The numbers describe the suspension and resolution as interval classes, so compound intervals can receive the same analytical label.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 10.9 labels the Barber example 4–3 and explains reduction of compound intervals in suspension labels. The revised card does not require the sounding interval to occupy a literal simple-fourth register.

concepts.label: Adagio for Strings
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hear how a 4–3 suspension delays resolution in Barber's work.

relations.note: The named score example is explicitly introduced as a 4–3 suspension.

concepts.card: The Neapolitan chord is a major chord built on the lowered second scale degree. In classical tonal analysis it commonly appears in first inversion and serves a predominant function. Its distinctive chromatic color therefore has a directional role, helping prepare the approach to dominant harmony.

evidence.note: Section 20.1 names flat II, most-common first inversion and predominant function; major quality follows the uppercase chord notation, not a claim that every flat-II sonority has this function.

concepts.label: Neapolitan chord
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize the flattened-supertonic major chord as a chromatic predominant.

relations.note: The Neapolitan's predominant role contrasts with the cadential six-four's dominant role, despite both often occurring near a cadence.

concepts.card: An augmented sixth chord contains notes a semitone below and above the dominant scale degree. The raised fourth moves upward while the lowered sixth moves downward toward dominant pitches. This characteristic voice-leading explains the chord family's predominant role in the cited tonal framework.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 21.1 states simultaneous semitone approaches to scale degree five and predominant function. Revised wording avoids describing the voices as converging in register; it only states the supported pitch-class movements.

concepts.label: Augmented sixth chord
concepts.learning_takeaway: Follow two chromatic voices approaching the dominant from opposite semitone directions.

relations.note: Both are chromatic predominant devices, but their construction differs: semitone approaches to dominant pitches versus a lowered-supertonic major triad.

concepts.card: Species counterpoint teaches melodic combination through restricted rhythmic relationships. Exercises can place one, two, three or four notes against a note in another voice. The cited textbook focuses on two voices, while noting that a longer college course may extend the method to four.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 30.1 explicitly describes rhythmic ratios, its two-voice focus and up to four voices in a semester course. No uninspected claim of a staged educational or coordination benefit remains.

concepts.label: Species counterpoint
concepts.learning_takeaway: Learn how controlled note ratios organize practice in combining independent melodies.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly presents species counterpoint as a method for learning contrapuntal composition.

concepts.card: Counterpoint combines two or more melodic lines sounding at the same time. A listener can follow their separate motion while also hearing the resulting texture. This differs from organizing the music principally as one foreground melody with accompaniment, a contrast the textbook calls contrapuntal versus homophonic.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 30.1 supplies simultaneous melodic lines and the texture contrast; independent motion is not taken to mean harmonic unrelatedness.

imported_records.description: compositional technique based on the combination of several overlapping melodic lines

concepts.label: Counterpoint
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish simultaneous melodic lines from a melody with accompaniment.
concepts.original_description: compositional technique based on the combination of several overlapping melodic lines

relations.note: The same section identifies species as a structured approach to composing counterpoint.

concepts.card: A small loudspeaker may reproduce a bass note's upper harmonics while barely producing its lowest frequency. Listeners can nevertheless hear the corresponding low pitch. For periodic tones, the spacing between surviving harmonics supplies information about the absent fundamental, so perceived pitch need not match the lowest audible component.

evidence.locator: Pitch, frequency, harmonics and missing fundamental
evidence.note: UNSW FAQ explains periodic-tone pitch from harmonic spacing and the bass-speaker example; it does not claim that arbitrary inharmonic sounds imply a unique missing fundamental.

concepts.label: Missing fundamental
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why a bass pitch remains audible when a speaker omits its fundamental.

relations.note: The source uses the missing fundamental to distinguish perceived pitch from the presence of a lowest-frequency component.

concepts.card: Piano octaves are often tuned slightly wider than a strict two-to-one frequency ratio. Stiff strings have upper partials sharper than ideal harmonics. Matching the upper note to a lower string's second partial can reduce audible beating, making a mathematically exact octave a poor practical match.

evidence.note: UNSW FAQ gives stretched second partials and beat-eliminating tuning; often and can avoid prescribing one exact stretch for every piano or register.

concepts.label: Stretch tuning
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain slightly widened piano octaves through the inharmonicity of stiff strings.

relations.note: The FAQ explicitly explains stretched tuning as a response to stiffness-induced inharmonicity in struck piano strings.

concepts.card: Two notes can give rise to an additional difference tone at the difference between their frequencies. Called a Tartini tone in music, it can result from nonlinear interactions in an instrument or the hearing system. The extra perceived pitch need not be one of the two notes originally played.

evidence.note: UNSW discusses difference-frequency combination tones and multiple possible nonlinear sources; can avoids attributing every case to one anatomical or instrumental mechanism.

concepts.label: Tartini tone
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify a difference tone produced by nonlinear interaction of two frequencies.

relations.note: A difference tone involves nonlinear frequency combination, whereas sympathetic resonance transfers energy into a compatible existing resonance; the comparison distinguishes two additional-sound phenomena.

concepts.card: Just intonation favors intervals described by simple frequency ratios. Yet pure fifths and pure thirds do not fit every chain of notes identically: repeated three-to-two fifths can conflict with a pure third. Fixed-pitch instruments must therefore confront compromises that adjustable voices or strings can handle differently.

evidence.locator: What is all the fuss about temperament?
evidence.note: UNSW temperament discussion supplies the chain-of-fifths mismatch and fixed versus adjustable instrument distinction; no claim that one tuning is universally best.

concepts.label: Just intonation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore why pure small-ratio intervals create compromises when changing keys.

relations.note: The FAQ directly contrasts just intonation with meantone's compromise between thirds and fifths.

concepts.card: Meantone temperament narrows fifths to improve the tuning of major thirds. The discrepancy is distributed across a chain of fifths rather than left entirely in the resulting third. This can suit particular keys well, while movement into other keys exposes the compromise's limits.

evidence.locator: What is all the fuss about temperament?
evidence.note: UNSW's worked example describes thirds improved by narrowing four fifths and worsening problems in other keys; no relation is made to personality temperament Q80157.

concepts.label: Meantone temperament
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how slightly narrowed fifths improve thirds but constrain modulation.

relations.note: The cited tuning comparison presents meantone as a different way to reconcile pure-interval demands on fixed-pitch instruments.

concepts.card: An open pipe behaves acoustically as though it extends slightly beyond its physical opening. The air's motion spreads outward before the pressure reflection develops, increasing the effective vibrating length. A resonance therefore occurs slightly lower than a simple model using only the measured tube length predicts.

evidence.note: UNSW End effects explains delayed reflection and effective length; slightly and simple model preserve the approximation rather than asserting one universal correction distance.

concepts.label: Wind-instrument end correction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why an open pipe resonates as though it were slightly longer.

relations.note: End corrections qualify ideal pipe predictions, including the simplified boundary-condition model used to explain clarinet register spacing.

concepts.card: A simple clarinet model is a cylindrical pipe closed at one end, which supports an odd-harmonic sequence. Its next resonance is therefore near three times the fundamental, a musical twelfth higher. Real clarinets depart from the ideal cylinder, but the model explains their characteristic register jump.

evidence.note: UNSW explicitly compares closed and open pipes and cautions that bore, bell, mouthpiece and end corrections complicate real instruments; no exact all-register harmonic claim.

concepts.label: Clarinet overblowing at the twelfth
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare a clarinet's next register with a flute's octave using boundary conditions.

relations.note: The article directly applies the closed-pipe approximation to clarinet register behavior.

concepts.card: A prepared piano changes its sound through objects placed beneath or between its strings. John Cage used such physical alterations to expand the instrument's available timbres. The keys remain a familiar interface, while the altered vibrating system produces sounds unlike those of an unprepared grand piano.

evidence.note: John Cage Trust explains objects placed among a grand piano's strings and the resulting transformed instrument; no invented preparation materials or exact acoustic mechanism is specified.

concepts.label: Prepared piano
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hear how objects placed between piano strings transform its available timbres.

relations.note: The Trust explicitly connects its prepared-piano samples with materials used for Cage's Sonatas and Interludes.

concepts.card: Benjamin Franklin's glass armonica uses glass bowls of different sizes mounted on a spinning axle. A player's touch sustains their vibration through friction, much as a damp finger can make a glass rim sing. The instrument turns that small physical effect into a playable arrangement of pitches.

evidence.locator: Why does rubbing your finger around the rim of a wine glass make a note?
evidence.note: UNSW wineglass explanation names Franklin, rotating bowls and finger-driven stick-slip; no claim about exact construction dimensions or historical priority beyond the source.

concepts.label: Glass armonica
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect friction-driven glass vibration with Franklin's rotating-bowl instrument.

relations.note: The source compares rubbing glass with a violin bow's sticking and slipping, providing a factual basis for comparing friction-driven sound production.

concepts.card: John Cage's 4′33″ directs attention toward sounds already present around a performance. The John Cage Trust's official app makes this idea concrete by recording ambient sound in three movements. The example shifts attention from supplying a new melody to noticing the listening environment itself.

evidence.note: The Trust's description supports ambient listening and its three-movement app realization; wording does not infer every original score instruction from the app or claim literal absence of sound.

concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore a three-movement performance that directs attention toward ambient sound.

relations.note: The Trust identifies this as Cage's composition; its ambient-sound focus offers a boundary-testing example of musical listening.

concepts.card: Cage's Sonatas and Interludes, composed in 1946–48, uses a prepared piano whose strings are altered by inserted materials. The John Cage Trust later supervised samples made with the work's actual preparation materials, linking the composition's identity to a particular physically modified sound source.

evidence.note: The Trust gives dates, work title and supervised sampling using actual preparation materials; no unsupported list of objects or formal analysis of the cycle is added.

concepts.label: Sonatas and Interludes
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect a particular Cage cycle with reproducible preparations altering piano sound.

relations.note: The official description explicitly identifies the work's piano preparations as the basis for its supervised sampled sounds.

concepts.card: Johann Joseph Fux's Gradus ad Parnassum (1725) teaches contrapuntal composition through species counterpoint. The cited textbook explains this approach through one, two, three or four notes against another voice's note. The work offers a historical example of organizing musical instruction around constrained rhythmic relationships.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 30.1 gives Fux, 1725 and species pedagogy with rhythmic relationships. The revised wording does not imply that first species necessarily places a note against a longer note or claim a measured instructional outcome.

concepts.label: Gradus ad Parnassum
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore Fux's historical organization of contrapuntal practice into rhythmic species.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly states that Fux's work teaches composition through species counterpoint.

concepts.card: Memory involves several activities rather than a single recording process. Encoding organizes incoming information, storage retains it, and retrieval brings it back for use. Remembering a fact later therefore depends on more than exposure: the information must have been encoded and remain accessible when needed.

evidence.note: OpenStax 8.1 defines encoding, storage and retrieval; the final consequence follows that sequence without claiming a literal computer-like architecture is complete.

imported_records.description: mental faculties and processes involved in storing and retrieving information
imported_records.subsection: Anthropology, psychology and everyday life / Psychology

concepts.label: Memory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish encoding, retaining and recovering information rather than treating memory as a recording.
concepts.original_description: mental faculties and processes involved in storing and retrieving information

relations.note: The chapter explicitly includes procedural skill memory among the forms of long-term memory.

concepts.card: Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model treats temporary mental activity as more than a single storage box. A central executive coordinates specialized systems for verbal and visual-spatial material. The later addition of an episodic buffer illustrates that this is a developing explanatory model, not an immutable anatomical diagram.

evidence.note: OpenStax 8.1 names the executive, subsystems and Baddeley 2000 buffer addition; explicitly a model, without unsupported localization or claims that the buffer belonged to the 1974 formulation.

concepts.label: Working memory model
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore a model that separates temporary verbal and visual-spatial processing under executive control.

relations.note: The chapter introduces this as an alternative explanatory model of memory's short-term organization.

concepts.card: Sensory memory briefly holds information from sights, sounds and other sensory events. In the Atkinson–Shiffrin model, this fleeting store precedes short-term memory. The distinction explains why a sensory trace can exist momentarily without becoming something retained for later conscious recall.

evidence.note: OpenStax 8.1 Sensory Memory supports brief traces and model placement; preserve the baseline's original description separately rather than silently replacing its wording.

imported_records.description: bodily experienced sensations from the past

concepts.label: Sensory memory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish very brief sensory persistence from longer-term storage.
concepts.original_description: bodily experienced sensations from the past

relations.note: The textbook explicitly describes sensory memory as a stage within a model of memory storage.

concepts.card: The self-reference effect is a relative memory advantage for information connected to oneself. Material considered in personally relevant terms can be remembered better than less self-relevant material. It is studied as an influence on encoding, linking what information means to a person with later remembering.

evidence.note: OpenStax Encoding defines the relative advantage and places it after semantic-processing experiments; can avoids an exceptionless guarantee or an instructional prescription.

concepts.label: Self-reference effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Investigate why relating information to oneself can improve later remembering.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly introduces self-reference as an effect on encoding and subsequent memory.

concepts.card: Procedural memory is expressed in skilled actions, such as balancing on a bicycle or driving. Practice can improve performance even when a person cannot fully describe the knowledge guiding it. This distinguishes remembering how to do something from consciously reporting facts or past events.

evidence.note: OpenStax Long-Term Memory defines implicit procedural skill and contrasts reportable explicit memories; not every component of driving is claimed unconscious.

concepts.label: Procedural memory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish remembering how to perform a skill from verbally recalling its instructions.

relations.note: Molaison's preserved improvement despite impaired new declarative memory provides a concrete comparison between performance-based and consciously reportable remembering.

concepts.card: Proactive interference occurs when older learning gets in the way of remembering newer information. After changing phone numbers, you might keep giving the old number automatically. The direction matters: an established memory is obstructing access to its more recently learned replacement.

evidence.note: OpenStax 8.3 defines old-to-new interference and gives the phone-number example; this concerns retrieval competition, not proof that the new memory was erased.

concepts.label: Proactive interference
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how an older memory can obstruct recall of newly learned information.

relations.note: The source explicitly distinguishes the two forms by whether older or newer information interferes.

concepts.card: Retroactive interference occurs when newer learning makes older information harder to recall. After learning a replacement address, you might struggle to recover the previous one. The direction reverses proactive interference: what was learned later now obstructs access to what was learned earlier.

evidence.note: OpenStax 8.3 defines new-to-old interference and depicts new and old email addresses; harder to recall does not assert permanent erasure.

concepts.label: Retroactive interference
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how later learning can obstruct access to older information.

relations.note: The chapter presents retroactive and proactive interference as opposite directions of interference between old and new learning.

concepts.card: A source-monitoring error confuses where remembered information came from. Someone might remember seeing a film accurately but assign that experience to the wrong companion. The mistake concerns the memory's origin or context, showing why recognizing a familiar detail does not guarantee correct attribution.

evidence.note: OpenStax misattribution example supports wrong companion/context. Only registered Q7565103 is used; no second meaning is asserted for Q6875176 and no silent baseline merger occurs.

imported_records.description: type of memory error

concepts.label: Source-monitoring error
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize a remembered detail whose origin has been confused.
concepts.original_description: type of memory error

relations.note: Confusing a remembered source differs from incorporating misleading later information, although both can distort reports about an event.

concepts.card: Later information can alter how an earlier event is remembered. In Loftus and Palmer's car-crash studies, wording in questions affected speed estimates and later reports of broken glass. The finding shows how post-event suggestions can shape reports, rather than proving that every eyewitness memory is inaccurate.

evidence.note: OpenStax describes both question wording and later glass reports; studies plural avoids treating the different experimental stages as one undifferentiated sample.

concepts.label: Misinformation effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how misleading information after an event can alter later reports.

relations.note: These are different routes to memory distortion: external post-event suggestion versus confusion over a detail's source.

concepts.card: Henry Molaison, known in research as H. M., had severe difficulty forming new declarative memories after brain surgery. Yet he could improve at repeatedly practiced tasks without remembering previous practice. His case separates conscious memory for an episode from learning expressed through better performance.

evidence.note: PubMed abstract of Augustinack et al. directly identifies Henry Molaison as H. M.; OpenStax 8.2 supports surgery and declarative impairment, and 8.3 supports improved performance without recalled practice. Do not claim all old memories remained intact.
Identifies H. M. and the effect of his operation on declarative memory; does not supply his full name.
Directly identifies Henry Molaison as H. M. and describes the operation causing his amnesia.

concepts.label: Henry Molaison
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare impaired new declarative memories with preserved improvement on practiced tasks.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly uses H. M. to contrast impaired new episodic/semantic memory with preserved procedural learning.

concepts.card: An absolute sensory threshold is usually defined as the stimulus intensity detected on half of repeated presentations under specified conditions. It is therefore a probabilistic measurement, not a magical boundary below which detection never happens. The testing conditions matter when comparing how sensitive different observers appear.

evidence.note: OpenStax 5.1 supplies the fifty-percent criterion and controlled conditions; probabilistic interpretation follows that definition without importing unsupported exact sensitivity estimates.
Provides the decision-theoretic premise for the editorial comparison.

concepts.label: Absolute sensory threshold
concepts.learning_takeaway: Interpret detection threshold as a probability under controlled conditions.

relations.note: A detection percentage alone does not separate available sensory information from a decision criterion; signal detection theory analyzes that distinction.

concepts.card: A just-noticeable difference measures the change needed to distinguish two stimulus intensities. The same added light can be conspicuous in a dark room yet barely noticeable in bright surroundings. This differs from asking whether any light can be detected at all, the question behind an absolute threshold.

evidence.note: OpenStax 5.1 contrasts difference and absolute thresholds using dark versus bright settings; avoid treating Weber's approximate scaling as universal across every intensity range.

concepts.label: Just-noticeable difference
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why noticing a change depends on the starting stimulus intensity.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly distinguishes detecting a stimulus from detecting a difference between stimuli.

concepts.card: With prolonged stimulation, a continuing sensory input can become less noticeable even while it remains present. OpenStax describes this as sensory adaptation. The change highlights a gap between continuing stimulation and conscious experience, helping explain why an initially prominent feature of the surroundings can fade from awareness.

evidence.note: OpenStax's perception section explicitly describes reduced notice during continued stimulation; this phenomenological card does not assert a particular receptor mechanism or equate every attention lapse with adaptation.

concepts.label: Sensory adaptation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish continuing sensory stimulation from reduced conscious notice over time.

relations.note: Reduced notice of sustained input differs from missing a visible unexpected event while concentrating on another task.

concepts.card: Inattentional blindness is missing a visible event while attention is occupied elsewhere. In the basketball-pass counting demonstration described by OpenStax, many viewers failed to notice an unexpected gorilla-costumed figure.
