The result concerns divided task demands, not an inability of the eyes to receive the image.

evidence.note: OpenStax 5.1 gives the counting task and unexpected figure; many avoids transferring one condition's numerical rate to every observer or task.

concepts.label: Inattentional blindness
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how a visible unexpected event can escape notice during another task.

relations.note: OpenStax explicitly presents the unexpected-figure demonstration as evidence that attention affects perception of the environment; inattentional blindness is the named perceptual failure in that discussion.

concepts.card: Signal detection theory separates sensory evidence from the criterion for reporting a signal. With evidence quality held fixed, lowering the criterion can increase both hits and false alarms; raising it can reduce both. Better sensitivity and greater willingness to answer yes are different changes.

evidence.note: Heeger’s Information and Criterion discussion and Figures 2–4 distinguish changing a criterion along one ROC from changing evidence quality. The revised card explicitly holds information fixed for the criterion tradeoff and makes no clinical recommendation.
Separates information quality and decision criterion, and shows the hit/false-alarm tradeoff.

concepts.label: Signal detection theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore detecting a target among noise when expectations and task goals influence reports.

relations.note: A fifty-percent detection threshold summarizes responses, while signal detection theory distinguishes evidence quality from the criterion behind those responses.

concepts.card: Figure–ground organization separates a focal object from its background. In the familiar vase-and-faces image, the same boundary can outline a white vase or two dark faces. Changing which region counts as the figure changes what the image seems to depict.

evidence.note: Section 5.6, figure-ground paragraph and Figure 5.25, support segmentation and the reversible vase/faces example; the card avoids claiming that segmentation must always precede recognition.

imported_records.description: humans' ability to separate foreground from background in visual images

concepts.label: Figure–ground (perception)
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why a single image can reverse between an object and its background.
concepts.original_description: humans' ability to separate foreground from background in visual images

relations.note: Compare selecting an object against its background with perceptually completing an incomplete object; these are distinct operations illustrated in the same Gestalt discussion.

concepts.card: Perceptual closure is the tendency to see a complete object from incomplete visual parts. Broken arcs can look like a circle rather than unrelated segments. The perceived whole therefore contains an organization that is not supplied by a continuous drawn outline.

evidence.note: Section 5.6, closure definition and Figure 5.29, explicitly contrast whole circles and rectangles with fragmented segments; this is a perceptual tendency, not a guarantee for any broken image.

concepts.label: Perceptual closure
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how incomplete parts can be perceived as a complete object.

relations.note: Closure fills an incomplete whole, whereas good continuation favors smooth trajectories; comparing their illustrations prevents treating all visual grouping as one mechanism.

concepts.card: Good continuation is a visual grouping tendency: lines that form a smooth path are more likely to be perceived as belonging together than jagged, broken alternatives. It helps explain why an arrangement of separate marks can appear organized into continuous trajectories.

evidence.note: Section 5.6 calls continuity a tendency toward smooth flowing lines; the card keeps probabilistic wording and does not claim a compulsory rule of vision.

concepts.label: Good continuation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why smooth continuations are often grouped rather than broken alternatives.

relations.note: The continuity and closure examples invite comparison between following a smooth path and completing an object from missing pieces, without identifying the two principles.

concepts.card: A mental set is persistence with a problem-solving approach that worked before but is ineffective now. Familiarity can keep a solver repeating the same strategy instead of reconsidering the problem. Functional fixedness is a particular case involving an object's expected use.

evidence.note: Section 7.3 defines persistence with an earlier successful approach and explicitly calls functional fixedness a type of mental set; no claim that all learned routines are harmful.

concepts.label: Mental set
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize persistence with a formerly useful approach after circumstances change.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies functional fixedness as a type of mental set, narrowing a habitual strategy to assumptions about object use.

concepts.card: Functional fixedness restricts thinking about an object to its usual purpose. In Duncker's candle problem, seeing a box only as a container can obscure its use as a candle support. Overcoming that restriction requires reconsidering what the available materials can do.

evidence.note: Section 7.3, Duncker problem and Figure 7.10, support the box's alternative use; the prose avoids repeating the source's apparent typo about using fixedness to overcome the problem.

concepts.label: Functional fixedness
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how an object's conventional use can hide an alternative solution.

relations.note: The source expressly describes functional fixedness as a kind of mental set: a familiar use constrains the attempted solution.

concepts.card: Anchoring occurs when one piece of information receives disproportionate weight in judgment. A house hunter may fixate on an initial spending figure and overlook what that amount actually buys. The focal value narrows consideration even when other relevant information is available.

evidence.note: Section 7.3's housing-budget example supports overfocus on a focal amount; this card does not claim a measured universal numerical adjustment effect from that example alone.

imported_records.description: an effect where an individual depends too heavily on an initial piece of information when making decisions

concepts.label: Anchoring effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Investigate how an initial focal value can steer subsequent judgment.
concepts.original_description: an effect where an individual depends too heavily on an initial piece of information when making decisions

relations.note: Compare overreliance on a focal information point with reliance on a readily accessible example; both can narrow consideration, but their selection mechanisms differ.

concepts.card: Confirmation bias makes evidence supporting an existing belief easier to notice than evidence challenging it. Someone convinced a teacher is unfriendly may remember curt exchanges while overlooking pleasant ones. The resulting impression can feel well supported because counterexamples received less attention.

evidence.note: Section 7.3's professor example supports selective attention to confirming episodes; retain authored control local:authored:000049 and its prior version, with Q431498 left as a historical equivalence proposal rather than a second meaning.

imported_records.description: Examining the tendency to favor information that supports existing beliefs.

concepts.label: Confirmation bias
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize selective attention to information supporting an existing belief.
concepts.original_description: Examining the tendency to favor information that supports existing beliefs.

relations.note: Confirmation bias favors evidence fitting a prior belief; the availability heuristic favors accessible examples. This comparison separates two reasons an evidence sample may be selective.

concepts.card: Hindsight bias is the tendency to see a known outcome as having been predictable beforehand. Learning what happened changes the perspective from which an earlier decision is judged. Confidence after the event can therefore be mistaken for foresight that was never actually demonstrated.

evidence.note: Section 7.3 defines hindsight as retrospective predictability; the temporal contrast is explanatory paraphrase, not a claim that every correct retrospective explanation is biased.

imported_records.description: tendency to perceive past events as more predictable than they actually were at the time

concepts.label: Hindsight bias
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish knowing an outcome from having predicted it beforehand.
concepts.original_description: tendency to perceive past events as more predictable than they actually were at the time

relations.note: Hindsight concerns a known outcome's apparent predictability; confirmation concerns selecting support for an existing belief. Their juxtaposition separates retrospective confidence from selective evidence use.

concepts.card: The availability heuristic uses readily accessible examples or recent experiences to guide judgment. That shortcut can be misleading when the easiest case to recall is poorly suited to the decision. Accessibility supplies an answer quickly, but does not establish that the example is representative.

evidence.note: Section 7.3 explicitly says the available example may not best inform a decision; representativeness here means suitability of evidence, not the separate representativeness heuristic.

imported_records.description: tendency and mental shortcut of preferring an item with more available information

concepts.label: Availability heuristic
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how accessible examples substitute for broader evidence in judgment.
concepts.original_description: tendency and mental shortcut of preferring an item with more available information

relations.note: A readily recalled case and a focal numerical amount can each dominate judgment for different reasons; the comparison does not merge the two biases.

concepts.card: Intrinsic motivation comes from satisfaction in the activity itself, such as baking because it is enjoyable. External rewards can also motivate the same person. Distinguishing these sources helps explain why turning a favorite activity into paid work can sometimes change its appeal.

evidence.note: Section 10.1's intrinsic/extrinsic distinction and Odessa baking example support mixed motives and a possible change after payment; sometimes preserves the section's later qualifications.

concepts.label: Intrinsic motivation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish doing an activity for satisfaction from doing it for an external reward.

relations.note: The section moves from intrinsic motivation to evidence that external rewards can change it, while distinguishing tangible rewards, praise and expectations.

concepts.card: External rewards can change intrinsic motivation rather than simply adding to it. Expected tangible rewards may weaken interest in an activity, while praise or an unexpected reward can have different effects. The finding depends on the reward and context, so payment does not invariably destroy enjoyment.

evidence.note: Section 10.1 distinguishes expected tangible rewards, praise and surprise; the card retains Q6917879 and does not create a second overjustification identity or universal causal law.

imported_records.description: theory in psychology and microeconomics

concepts.label: Motivation crowding theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine how external rewards can weaken or strengthen intrinsic motivation under different conditions.
concepts.original_description: theory in psychology and microeconomics

relations.note: The reward discussion directly concerns increases or decreases in intrinsic motivation, making this an interaction with that motive rather than a separate definition of enjoyment.

concepts.card: The Yerkes–Dodson relationship links arousal and performance while emphasizing task difficulty. A demanding task may be disrupted at an arousal level that suits a simple one. The useful lesson is not that moderate arousal always wins, but that an apparent optimum depends on the task.

evidence.note: Section 10.1 explicitly qualifies the middle-is-best simplification through difficulty; the card states a relationship and qualified example rather than a universal biological law or prescriptive stress target.

concepts.label: Yerkes–Dodson relationship
concepts.learning_takeaway: Investigate why task difficulty matters when relating arousal to performance.

relations.note: Compare performance's dependence on arousal and task difficulty with motivation's dependence on perceived capability; these are different explanations discussed in the motivation chapter.

concepts.card: Self-efficacy is a person's belief that they can carry out a particular task. In Bandura's account, this belief helps shape the challenges people attempt and their persistence after setbacks. Believing an outcome is valuable differs from believing one has the capability to achieve it.

evidence.note: Section 10.1 defines task-specific capability beliefs and attributes their motivational role to Bandura; the card does not equate confidence with actual skill or guarantee success.

concepts.label: Self-efficacy
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish believing one can complete a task from valuing its reward.

relations.note: Capability beliefs answer whether one can perform a task, whereas intrinsic motivation concerns satisfaction in doing it; the chapter supports both premises without identifying them.

concepts.card: Cognitive dissonance is discomfort associated with inconsistent beliefs, attitudes or behavior. Someone who smokes while believing smoking is harmful may reduce the conflict by quitting or by discounting the evidence. Resolving the discomfort can therefore involve changing behavior or changing its interpretation.

evidence.note: Section 12.3's definition, smoking example and Figure 12.11 support both routes; the card avoids making the source's restrictive self-image formulation a universal necessary condition.

imported_records.description: mental stress or discomfort experienced by an individual who holds two or more contradictory beliefs, ideas, or values at the same time

concepts.label: Cognitive dissonance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore responses to discomfort when commitments and behavior conflict.
concepts.original_description: mental stress or discomfort experienced by an individual who holds two or more contradictory beliefs, ideas, or values at the same time

relations.note: Discounting conflicting evidence can be compared with selectively attending to confirming evidence, but discomfort reduction and confirmation bias remain distinct explanatory subjects.

concepts.card: The elaboration likelihood model distinguishes persuasion through evaluating a message's arguments from persuasion through peripheral cues. A buyer might compare safety evidence or respond to a celebrity endorsement. The model connects these routes with the audience's motivation and effort in processing the message.

evidence.note: Section 12.3, Figure 12.15 and central/peripheral route paragraphs, support argument evaluation, endorsement cues and processing effort; the card identifies a model rather than an exhaustive settled binary for all persuasion.

concepts.label: Elaboration likelihood model
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare evaluating an argument with responding to peripheral cues.

relations.note: The model concerns how a persuasive message is processed; foot-in-the-door concerns the sequence of requests. Their comparison distinguishes explanatory route from influence procedure.

concepts.card: The foot-in-the-door technique begins with a small request before asking for something larger. In Freedman and Fraser's study, people who first accepted a small sign or petition were more likely to accept a large yard sign. This was an experimental tendency, not guaranteed compliance.

evidence.note: Section 12.3 describes the 1966 sign/petition comparison; the final sentence preserves probabilistic scope and avoids presenting a guaranteed method of controlling another person.

concepts.label: Foot-in-the-door technique
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore the qualified finding that a small request can precede increased agreement to a larger one.

relations.note: Compare a request-sequencing procedure with a model of message processing. Both concern persuasion, but the cited section does not make one an instance of the other.

concepts.card: In Asch's line-judgment experiments, participants heard a group give an obviously wrong answer before responding aloud. Many agreed with the group at least once. Dissenting allies and private responding changed conformity, showing that agreement depended partly on the social arrangement of the task.

evidence.note: Section 12.4 supports confederates' wrong answers, public responses and effects of dissent/privacy; many avoids generalizing one percentage to all studies or people.

concepts.label: Asch's conformity experiments
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine public agreement with a clearly mistaken majority in a particular experimental setting.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly interprets conformity in the unambiguous Asch task as fitting in and avoiding ridicule, an instance of normative influence.

concepts.card: Normative social influence draws people toward a group's position because acceptance matters. Someone may publicly give an answer they privately doubt to avoid ridicule or fit in. Agreement in this case need not mean believing the group has better information about the question.

evidence.locator: Why conform? normative versus informational influence
evidence.note: Section 12.4 distinguishes fitting in from information-based conformity and notes public agreement without private acceptance in Asch's setting; the card allows rather than requires private disagreement.

concepts.label: Normative social influence
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish joining a group to gain acceptance from believing its answer is correct.

relations.note: The text explicitly contrasts acceptance-seeking with trusting the group's information, identifying two different motivations for conformity.

concepts.card: Informational social influence occurs when people treat others' responses as evidence about an uncertain situation. If smoke in a theater might be a special effect, nearby people's reactions can guide interpretation. Conformity here reflects reliance on presumed knowledge, rather than only a wish to belong.

evidence.locator: Why conform? normative versus informational influence
evidence.note: Section 12.4's ambiguous smoke example and competent-group definition support uncertainty-driven reliance; the hypothetical example is not presented as a measured emergency experiment.

concepts.label: Informational social influence
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand relying on others as information when a situation is ambiguous.

relations.note: The textbook directly distinguishes believing the group is informed from seeking its acceptance, while allowing both as motivations for conformity.

concepts.card: Milgram's participants believed they were administering increasingly strong shocks when an experimenter instructed them to continue; the learner actually received none. In the original setting, many continued to the highest level. Changing the setting or bringing the learner closer reduced obedience, limiting any simple universal conclusion.

evidence.note: Section 12.4 describes the deceptive shock setup and lower continuation rates in office/proximity variants; no claim that all participants obeyed or that this settles explanations of historical atrocities.

concepts.label: Milgram's obedience experiments
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare obedience in the original setup with changes produced by proximity and setting.

relations.note: Milgram tests responses to an experimenter's commands, whereas Asch tests responses to a group's judgments. The comparison distinguishes authority-directed obedience from peer conformity.

concepts.card: Psychology studies mind and behavior through empirical methods. Mental processes are not directly visible, so researchers draw inferences from behavior, biological indicators and people's reports. A claim about thought becomes scientifically testable by connecting it to observations that could support or challenge an explanation.

evidence.note: Section 1.1 explicitly links indirect mental inference to observable behavior, biological indicators and self-report; the card does not imply that introspection alone proves a mental mechanism.

imported_records.description: study of mental functions and behaviours
imported_records.subsection: Anthropology, psychology and everyday life / Psychology

concepts.label: Psychology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how observable behavior and reports support inferences about mental processes.
concepts.original_description: study of mental functions and behaviours

relations.note: Inferring an unobservable psychological process from a measure creates the construct-validity question: does that measure capture the intended concept? The two inspected sections supply these premises.

concepts.card: Inter-rater reliability concerns agreement between observers evaluating the same event. If two researchers classify a behavior differently, the coding procedure may be inconsistent. Agreement helps establish reproducibility across observers, but by itself does not show that their shared measure captures the intended psychological construct.

evidence.note: Section 2.3 defines observer agreement and distinguishes reliability from validity; the coding example applies that definition without claiming agreement proves accuracy.

concepts.label: Inter-rater reliability
concepts.learning_takeaway: Check whether different observers classify the same behavior consistently.

relations.note: The source lists inter-rater and test–retest reliability as distinct consistency checks: across observers versus across administrations.

concepts.card: Test–retest reliability asks whether a measure produces consistent results across repeated administrations. It evaluates stability over occasions, whereas inter-rater reliability evaluates agreement among observers. A repeatable score can still measure the wrong thing, so consistency alone does not establish the validity of its interpretation.

evidence.note: Section 2.3 distinguishes repeated-administration consistency from observer agreement and states that reliability does not entail validity; the card does not demand unchanged scores when the actual trait changes.

concepts.label: Test–retest reliability
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish stability across repeated measurements from agreement among observers.

relations.note: Both forms are explicitly listed in the same reliability passage, with different sources of variation being checked.

concepts.card: Construct validity asks whether a measure actually captures the concept it is intended to represent. A procedure can produce consistent scores yet miss its intended target. The challenge is therefore more than repeatability: it is connecting an observable measurement to the psychological idea being studied.

evidence.note: Section 2.3 defines construct validity and separates validity from reliability; the card does not assert that surface plausibility or one correlation settles the question.

concepts.label: Construct validity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ask whether an operational measure captures the intended psychological concept.

relations.note: The source explicitly contrasts measuring the intended construct with merely obtaining consistent results; observer agreement is one specified form of that consistency.

concepts.card: In this research-methods sense, ecological validity concerns how well findings apply to ordinary settings. Unobtrusive observation of people in their usual surroundings can improve realism, but sacrifices experimental control. A realistic setting helps the applicability question without automatically answering every question about cause and effect.

evidence.note: Section 2.2's naturalistic-observation discussion supports realism, generalization and control tradeoffs; retain this cited sense rather than treating all uses of ecological validity as interchangeable.

concepts.label: Ecological validity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Assess how closely a research setting represents real-world behavior.

relations.note: Real-world applicability and accurate measurement of an intended construct are different validity questions; the comparison is a learning bridge, not a claim that one guarantees the other.

concepts.card: A researcher's expectations can influence how ambiguous observations are scored. Someone who knows which participants received an intervention may interpret borderline responses in its favor. Concealing group assignments from the scorer helps reduce this route of bias, without guaranteeing that every other source of error disappears.

evidence.note: Section 2.3's test-scoring example motivates observer blinding; helps reduce avoids the textbook's stronger implication that blinding alone removes all alternative explanations.

concepts.label: Experimenter expectancy bias
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how a researcher's expectations can shape interpretation of ambiguous responses.

relations.note: The source introduces researcher blinding to address experimenter expectations and then defines double blinding as concealing assignment from participants as well.

concepts.card: In a double-blind study, participants and the relevant researchers do not know which group each participant belongs to. Concealing assignments helps limit both participant expectations and experimenter expectations. It is a protection against those influences, not a substitute for sound sampling, measurement or comparison groups.

evidence.note: Section 2.3 defines concealed assignment for researchers and participants; the final limitation follows the chapter's separate design requirements and avoids claiming that blinding alone demonstrates causation.

concepts.label: Double-blind study
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare controlling participant expectations with controlling researcher expectations.

relations.note: Double blinding is directly introduced as controlling both experimenter and participant expectations, so its relation to expectancy bias is stated rather than inferred.

concepts.card: Research debriefing explains a study after participation, especially when its purpose was concealed. Participants receive an honest account of the research question, the use of their data and why deception was used. The explanation helps restore information that the study deliberately withheld during the task.

evidence.note: Section 2.4 explicitly requires a full explanation after deceptive studies, including purpose, data use, reasons and further information; the card does not promise that explanation erases any harm.

concepts.label: Research debriefing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why concealed research purposes must be explained after deceptive studies.

relations.note: The ethics passage makes debriefing a requirement following deception and specifies the information participants should receive.

concepts.card: Psychological studies sometimes conceal their precise purpose because knowing it could change participants' responses. That creates an ethical tension between informative behavior and informed participation. The cited ethics account limits deceptive procedures and requires a later explanation of the purpose, data use and reasons for concealment.

evidence.note: Section 2.4 explains response distortion and debriefing, with ethical limits; the card attributes this account and does not treat scientific convenience as sufficient permission for harmful deception.

concepts.label: Deception in psychological research
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine the tension between realistic responses and participants' knowledge of a study's purpose.

relations.note: The source directly connects permissible use of deception with a subsequent full debriefing rather than treating concealment as an unrestricted research tool.

concepts.card: Social desirability bias can make self-reports reflect how people want to appear rather than what they actually do or believe. A respondent might underreport drinking to seem more acceptable. This is one possible source of inaccurate survey answers, alongside memory errors and other influences.

evidence.note: Section 2.2's surveys paragraph explicitly separates lying, misremembering and answers intended to look good; the card does not diagnose every inaccurate response as deliberate dishonesty.

concepts.label: Social desirability bias
concepts.learning_takeaway: Consider why answers about behavior may reflect a wish to appear acceptable.

relations.note: Social desirability concerns the participant's presentation of an answer, whereas experimenter expectancy concerns the researcher's interpretation; contrasting them separates two locations where measurement can be distorted.

concepts.card: The doctrine of double effect distinguishes harm intended as a means from harm foreseen as a side effect of pursuing a good end. Its defenders also require proportionality and attention to avoiding harm. Merely saying a bad result was unintended does not make it permissible.

evidence.note: SEP sections 1 and 3 support the intention/foresight distinction, proportionality and harm minimization; attribution to defenders avoids presenting a contested doctrine as settled morality.

concepts.label: Doctrine of double effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish intending harm as a means from foreseeing it as a side effect.

relations.note: The entry explicitly warns that intended versus foreseen harm is a different distinction from doing versus allowing harm; neither distinction should be substituted for the other.

concepts.card: The problem of closeness challenges the line between intended means and foreseen side effects. A harmful result may be so closely connected with an agent's chosen means that calling it unintended seems artificial. The difficulty is classifying the action without already assuming the moral verdict.

evidence.note: SEP section 4.2 identifies closely connected harms, and 4.3 raises evaluation-driven descriptions; the card presents a criticism rather than declaring that every intention distinction collapses.

evidence.locator: Sections 4.2 The Problem of Closeness and 4.3 The Side Effect Effect
evidence.note: The closely connected harm problem and normative influence on action descriptions together support the classification concern.

concepts.label: Problem of closeness in double effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine when a harmful side effect seems inseparable from the agent's chosen means.

relations.note: The entry names the problem of closeness as a criticism of double effect's distinction between intended means and merely foreseen harms.

concepts.card: Doing harm and allowing harm distinguish bringing about a harmful outcome from failing to prevent it. Philosophers dispute their moral significance. Rachels's paired cases compare deliberate drowning with deliberately withholding rescue, testing whether the distinction alone can explain a difference in blame.

evidence.note: SEP sections 1–2 present Rachels's cases and objections to both their comparability and generalization; the card treats the cases as a test, not proof that killing and letting die are always equivalent.

concepts.label: Doing versus allowing harm
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate causing versus permitting harm from intention and from moral verdicts.

relations.note: The entry uses driver and bystander trolley variants to examine whether doing/allowing explains moral judgments, and records challenges to that explanation.

concepts.card: The trolley problem asks whether redirecting a lethal threat from five people toward one is permissible. Changing the decision-maker from driver to bystander challenges explanations based simply on doing versus allowing harm. The variants probe moral distinctions rather than supply an agreed algorithm for sacrifice.

evidence.locator: 3 The Trolley Problem and the Doing/Allowing Distinction
evidence.note: SEP section 3 recounts Foot's driver and Thomson's bystander variants and continuing disagreement; no endorsement of a universal permissibility verdict or practical sacrifice rule is made.

imported_records.description: thought experiment in ethics

concepts.label: Trolley problem
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare driver and bystander versions rather than assuming one explanation settles both.
concepts.original_description: thought experiment in ethics

relations.note: The bystander variant is explicitly discussed as a challenge to Foot's doing/allowing explanation of the driver's choice.

concepts.card: Moral luck names a tension in judging people: responsibility seems to require control, yet praise and blame often depend on factors outside their control. Two equally reckless actions can have different outcomes. The puzzle asks whether, and how, those differences should affect moral assessment.

evidence.locator: The Problem: Control Principle and moral assessment
evidence.note: SEP's Control Principle and resultant-luck examples support the tension; the card asks rather than settles the normative question and does not create an additional resultant-luck identity.

concepts.label: Moral luck
concepts.learning_takeaway: Investigate how moral assessment can depend on circumstances outside an agent's control.

relations.note: The entry identifies circumstantial luck as one form of moral luck, involving which situations a person happens to face rather than only how an action ends.

concepts.card: The problem of temporary intrinsics asks how one persisting object can have incompatible intrinsic properties at different times. A metal plate may change from round to square. Explaining that change requires an account of what it means to possess a property at a time.

evidence.note: SEP Identity Over Time sections 2.3–2.4 use the plate's shape change and discuss competing solutions; the card does not infer that ordinary change is logically impossible.

concepts.label: Problem of temporary intrinsics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ask how one persisting object can possess incompatible intrinsic properties at different times.

relations.note: The section explicitly frames the temporary-intrinsics problem through Leibniz's Law: identity and differing properties require explaining the temporal qualification.

concepts.card: Circumstantial moral luck concerns the unchosen situations that test a person's character. Someone placed in a brutal political environment may face choices another person never encounters. The philosophical problem is whether differing moral assessments are justified when the opportunity for wrongdoing itself depended on luck.

evidence.note: SEP's circumstantial-luck paragraph compares collaborators with imagined counterparts elsewhere; the card generalizes that structure without excusing atrocities or asserting that circumstances compel every action.

concepts.label: Circumstantial moral luck
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ask how unchosen situations expose people to different moral tests.

relations.note: Nagel's taxonomy in the entry expressly treats luck in one's circumstances as a kind of moral luck affecting assessment.

concepts.card: Constitutive moral luck concerns traits and dispositions shaped partly by factors people did not choose, including inheritance and upbringing. If those traits influence action, judging someone's character also raises a question about control. The issue is responsibility for who one has become, not merely what happens afterward.

evidence.note: SEP's constitutive-luck paragraphs identify genes, caregivers and peers, and connect dispositions with action; partly avoids a deterministic claim that character or conduct is wholly unchosen.

concepts.label: Constitutive moral luck
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine responsibility for dispositions shaped partly by unchosen development and inheritance.

relations.note: The source explicitly classifies luck in character and dispositions as constitutive moral luck, extending the control problem to agents as well as actions.

concepts.card: Supererogation is morally good action beyond what duty requires. A costly rescue may be admired even when failing to undertake it would not violate an obligation. Whether such optional goodness forms a genuine category is disputed, because some ethical theories make every morally best action compulsory.

evidence.note: SEP opening and Definition discuss good-but-not-required acts, heroic examples and theories denying the category; costly rescue is an illustration, not a requirement that every supererogatory act be costly.

concepts.label: Supererogation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore the possibility of morally good actions that duty does not require.

relations.note: The entry explicitly distinguishes optional action beyond duty from imperfect duties, which remain binding while allowing discretion over fulfillment, and notes attempts to equate them.

concepts.card: In the Kantian distinction discussed here, an imperfect duty remains obligatory while leaving latitude in how it is fulfilled. Flexibility about particular actions does not make the underlying duty optional. This separates discretion within an obligation from supererogation, which concerns morally good action beyond obligation.

evidence.note: SEP section 2 explicitly says imperfect duties are no less compelling and differ in application; the opening bounds this formulation to the Kantian discussion rather than every use of the term.

concepts.label: Imperfect duty
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish discretion over fulfilling a duty from permission to ignore it.

relations.note: The article contrasts imperfect duty's binding force and discretionary application with supererogatory optionality; it also acknowledges philosophers who dispute that separation.

concepts.card: Suberogation is a proposed category of morally bad but permissible conduct, conceived as a counterpart to good actions beyond duty. Ingratitude is sometimes offered as an example, but both the examples and the category are disputed. Badness and prohibited wrongdoing need not be treated as identical.

evidence.note: SEP section 2 describes the proposed mirror category, contested ingratitude example and difficulty identifying clear cases; proposed and sometimes preserve its disputed status.

concepts.label: Suberogation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Consider the disputed category of bad yet morally permitted conduct.

relations.note: The source introduces suberogation by asking whether supererogation has a mirror image, then examines why the suggested symmetry is controversial.

concepts.card: The justified true belief analysis proposes that knowledge requires a belief to be true and adequately justified, with those conditions together sufficient. Truth excludes error; justification excludes unsupported lucky guesses. Gettier cases challenge the proposal by combining justification and truth with another kind of epistemic luck.

evidence.note: SEP sections 1 and 3 describe the tripartite proposal and its challenge; proposes and challenge prevent the analysis from being presented as the settled definition of knowledge.

concepts.label: Justified true belief analysis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a belief's truth and justification in a traditional analysis of knowledge.

relations.note: The entry explicitly presents Gettier counterexamples as a challenge to the sufficiency of justification, truth and belief together.

concepts.card: The Gettier problem asks why some justified true beliefs still seem not to be knowledge. A person can reason from a justified but false premise to a conclusion that happens to be true for an unrelated reason. The success is accidental despite the apparent justification.

evidence.note: SEP section 3's Smith/Jones disjunction case supports justified false premise, valid inference and accidental truth; some and seem preserve the philosophical status of the counterexample judgment.

concepts.label: Gettier problem
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why a justified belief can be accidentally true yet fail to count as knowledge.

relations.note: Gettier cases are directly formulated as counterexamples to the traditional tripartite analysis, separating justified truth from nonaccidental knowledge.

concepts.card: The no-false-lemmas condition proposes repairing justified true belief by excluding beliefs inferred from false premises. It blocks some Gettier examples, but deceptive perceptual environments pose a further challenge. A belief can apparently be accidentally true without having been inferred from any false proposition.

evidence.note: SEP section 4 states the proposed fourth condition and noninferential counterexamples; the card does not claim the repair is accepted or sufficient.

concepts.label: No-false-lemmas condition
concepts.learning_takeaway: Evaluate the proposed repair that knowledge cannot be inferred from false premises.

relations.note: The entry expressly develops no false lemmas as an attempted additional condition for solving the Gettier problem, then presents objections.

concepts.card: In the fake-barn case, Henry happens to see a real barn in a landscape full of convincing facades. His belief is true and apparently justified, yet could easily have been mistaken. The example challenges whether accurate perception alone guarantees knowledge in a systematically deceptive environment.

evidence.note: SEP section 4's Barn County passage supplies Henry, the real barn and facades; apparently and challenges preserve the evaluative character of the knowledge verdict.

concepts.label: Fake-barn case
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how a deceptive environment can undermine otherwise accurate perception.

relations.note: The source presents Barn County as a challenge to the no-false-lemmas repair because Henry's belief need not involve inference from a false premise.

concepts.card: A sensitive belief tracks a counterfactual question: if the claim were false, would the person stop believing it? A mirage-based belief may fail because the same appearance would persuade without water. Sensitivity has been proposed as a condition on knowledge, but its adequacy is disputed.

evidence.note: SEP section 5.1 states the counterfactual and desert-water example, then discusses limitations; the card does not equate sensitivity with safety or endorse it as sufficient for knowledge.

concepts.label: Epistemic sensitivity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ask whether someone would stop believing a claim if it were false.

relations.note: Section 5.2 explicitly contrasts sensitivity with safety and explains why counterfactual contraposition does not make them equivalent.

concepts.card: A safe belief would not easily have been false: in nearby possible circumstances where the person holds it, it remains true. This proposed condition on knowledge differs from asking what the person would believe if the claim were false. What counts as nearby is itself contested.

evidence.note: SEP section 5.2 gives the nearby-worlds formulation and discusses vagueness of nearness; the card avoids treating safety as a settled necessary or sufficient condition.

concepts.label: Epistemic safety
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ask whether a belief could easily have been false in nearby circumstances.

relations.note: The source explicitly distinguishes safety's nearby true beliefs from sensitivity's response to falsity, noting that the two modal conditions are not equivalent.

concepts.card: Epistemic closure asks whether competent deduction preserves knowledge. On a common formulation, someone who retains knowledge of a premise and comes to believe its consequence by competent deduction knows that consequence. This is not a claim that people automatically know every implication of everything they know.

evidence.note: SEP section 1 rejects unqualified entailment closure and gives the competent-deduction principle with continued premise knowledge; the card presents a formulation within a disputed debate.

concepts.label: Epistemic closure
concepts.learning_takeaway: Investigate whether competent deduction from known premises preserves knowledge.

relations.note: Knowledge preservation under inference is a specific epistemological question; the closure entry and the broad account of cognitive success support this placement without implying universal acceptance of closure.

concepts.card: If high probability licenses belief, each ticket in a large fair lottery may reasonably be treated as a loser. Combining all those beliefs yields that every ticket loses, although one must win. The lottery paradox challenges combining individually plausible beliefs without restriction.

evidence.note: SEP section 3 presents Kyburg's acceptance rule and agglomeration conflict; the conditional opening avoids asserting that probability alone actually suffices for rational belief or knowledge.

concepts.label: Lottery paradox
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare rational acceptance of each likely loser with certainty that one ticket wins.

relations.note: The article introduces the preface paradox as a companion challenge to agglomeration, while noting that it does not require the same probabilistic acceptance rule.

concepts.card: An author can reasonably believe each carefully researched claim in a book while admitting that the book probably contains an error. Combining all the individual beliefs conflicts with that admission. The preface paradox tests how rational confidence in particular claims fits with recognition of one's fallibility.

evidence.note: SEP section 4 explains Makinson's author case and its conflict with agglomeration; the card preserves rational belief rather than recasting every assertion as knowledge or certainty.

concepts.label: Preface paradox
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine believing each researched claim while reasonably expecting some mistake in the whole book.

relations.note: The source connects both paradoxes through agglomeration while distinguishing the preface's ordinary recognition of fallibility from a numerical probability-acceptance rule.

concepts.card: Moore's paradox concerns the oddness of asserting a fact while denying that one believes it. The combination need not be logically contradictory: someone else could truthfully describe that situation. The puzzle is why the speaker's own present assertion appears to undermine the position it expresses.

evidence.note: SEP section 5.3 distinguishes first-person declarative oddity from third-person, conditional and past-tense counterparts; the card avoids calling the proposition itself a formal contradiction.

concepts.label: Moore's paradox
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why asserting a fact while denying belief in it sounds self-defeating.

relations.note: Both expose tensions involving belief, but Moore's case centers on an assertion's first-person stance, whereas the preface case concerns combining individually rational beliefs.

concepts.card: Meno's paradox asks how inquiry can work: if you already know the answer, inquiry seems unnecessary; if you do not, how could you recognize it? One response distinguishes partial knowledge from total ignorance. A searcher may know enough to recognize an answer without already possessing it.

evidence.note: SEP section 6.1 states the dilemma and partial-knowledge response; one response avoids presenting it as the only interpretation of Plato or the final resolution of all inquiry puzzles.

concepts.label: Meno's paradox of inquiry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Question how inquiry can recognize an answer it does not already know.

relations.note: A puzzle about gaining and recognizing knowledge belongs within epistemology's study of cognitive success; the bridge uses the inquiry passage and the field's inspected overview.

concepts.card: Epistemology investigates knowledge, justification, understanding and other kinds of cognitive success. It asks how evidence should constrain belief and what separates knowing from merely being right. Different approaches examine individual reasoning, sensory experience or the social interests that influence which evidence receives attention.

evidence.locator: Opening historical overview and cognitive-success definition
evidence.note: SEP's opening survey explicitly discusses knowledge versus true opinion, sensory justification, formal evidence constraints and feminist attention to interests; the card avoids reducing the field to one proposed knowledge analysis.

imported_records.description: Investigating knowledge, justification and the limits of understanding.

concepts.label: Epistemology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Investigate what distinguishes knowledge, justified belief and other forms of cognitive success.
concepts.original_description: Investigating knowledge, justification and the limits of understanding.

relations.note: The tripartite analysis is one particular attempt to explain knowledge within a broader field that also studies justification, understanding and evidence; it is not the definition of epistemology itself.

concepts.card: Numerical identity means being one and the same thing; qualitative identity means being alike in qualities. The distinction matters for change: a persisting object can remain the same object while its features alter. Similarity of appearance alone does not settle whether two descriptions pick out one thing.

evidence.note: SEP Identity Over Time section 1 distinguishes one object from exact resemblance and connects persistence with qualitative change; the card does not assume the controversial converse identity-of-indiscernibles principle.

concepts.label: Numerical and qualitative identity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish being one and the same object from being perfectly alike.

relations.note: The introduction moves directly from numerical/qualitative identity to Leibniz's Law, exposing the need to explain how qualitative change fits identity through time.

concepts.card: The indiscernibility of identicals says that if two names pick out the very same thing, every property of that thing must belong to both referents. It runs from identity to shared properties. The converse claim, that sharing all properties guarantees identity, is a different principle.

evidence.note: SEP section 1 explicitly distinguishes identity implying indiscernibility from the converse; the two-name formulation explains reference without suggesting that differing descriptions themselves prove distinct objects.

concepts.label: Indiscernibility of identicals
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why genuinely identical things cannot differ in a property.

relations.note: The entry states Leibniz's Law after distinguishing numerical from qualitative identity, and separately names its more controversial converse.

concepts.card: Relative identity proposes that asking whether two things are the same requires specifying the kind of thing: the same what? On Geach's view, things might be the same under one classification but different under another. This contested proposal challenges treating identity as a single unqualified relation.

evidence.note: SEP Identity Over Time section 1 attributes sortal-relative identity to Geach and contrasts it with absolute identity; proposes and contested prevent endorsing it as standard logic.

concepts.label: Relative identity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore the proposal that identity must answer same what rather than identity without qualification.

relations.note: Compare ordinary numerical identity with a proposal that identity must be qualified by a sortal. This is a competing analysis, not another name for qualitative similarity.

concepts.card: A clay statue raises a puzzle: the clay seems able to survive squashing, while the statue does not. Does that show two coincident objects, or should their relationship be understood differently? Material constitution investigates this disputed relationship between an object and the matter that constitutes it.

evidence.note: SEP opening and section 1 present the statue/lump persistence argument alongside identity and revisionary views; seems and the question explicitly avoid settling the dispute in favor of two objects.

concepts.label: Material constitution
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a statue from the material constituting it through their possible persistence conditions.

relations.note: The statue-and-clay argument explicitly invokes Leibniz's Law: if their persistence properties differ, identity is threatened. The entry presents rival responses rather than endorsing that inference without qualification.

concepts.card: Presentism holds that only temporally present objects exist. Merely past or future objects are excluded from its inventory of reality, though abstract entities may fall outside time. The claim concerns existence itself, not simply which events people can currently observe or remember.

evidence.locator: 6 Presentism, Eternalism, and the Growing Block Theory
evidence.note: SEP Time section 6 defines presentism and explicitly distinguishes temporal presence from spatial presence and timeless abstract objects; no claim that the past never occurred.

concepts.label: Presentism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore the thesis that only temporally present objects exist.

relations.note: The source directly opposes presentism to eternalism, which includes objects at past and future times in what exists.

concepts.card: Eternalism holds that past and future objects exist as well as present ones. An object can belong to reality without occupying the present moment. The disagreement with presentism concerns what exists, rather than whether past events are now occurring or can presently be observed.

evidence.locator: 6 Presentism, Eternalism, and the Growing Block Theory
evidence.note: SEP Time section 6 separates ontological existence from temporal location and includes past and future objects. The card avoids an extra spatial analogy and does not claim past events are happening at the present time.

concepts.label: Eternalism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish existing from being present when considering past and future objects.

relations.note: Section 6 explicitly defines eternalism as a way of opposing presentism's restriction of existence to present objects.

concepts.card: Growing block theory holds that the past and present exist, while the future does not yet exist. Reality expands as new events join its present edge. It differs from presentism, which excludes the past, and eternalism, which includes future objects in what exists.

evidence.locator: 6 Presentism, Eternalism, and the Growing Block Theory
evidence.note: SEP Time section 6 defines the increasing ontology and contrasts both alternatives; the card does not equate the growing block with four-dimensionalism or a settled physical theory.

concepts.label: Growing block theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore a temporal ontology in which the past and present exist but the future does not.

relations.note: The section contrasts eternalism's past-and-future existence with the growing block's past-and-present existence, marking the future as their key difference.

concepts.card: The sorites paradox turns tiny changes into a puzzle about vague categories. If one grain is not a heap, and adding one grain never makes the difference, repeated additions seem to imply that no heap is possible. Plausible small steps produce an unacceptable conclusion.

evidence.note: SEP opening and section 2 supply the grain-addition chain; the card identifies the conflict without asserting that the tolerance premise is true or resolving vagueness by definition.

concepts.label: Sorites paradox
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how apparently harmless small changes can generate a contradiction about vague categories.

relations.note: The entry presents epistemicism as one response to the sorites paradox, locating a sharp but unknowable boundary rather than accepting every small-step premise.

concepts.card: Epistemicism treats vagueness as a limit of knowledge rather than an absence of precise boundaries. There is, on this view, an exact cutoff between a heap and a non-heap, although we cannot identify it. Statements remain true or false even when their status is inaccessible.

evidence.note: SEP section 3.2 describes hidden sharp boundaries and preservation of bivalence; on this view makes the controversial account explicit rather than reporting it as a discovered linguistic fact.

concepts.label: Epistemicism about vagueness
concepts.learning_takeaway: Consider the view that vague categories have sharp boundaries we cannot know.

relations.note: The article presents epistemicism among responses to sorites, preserving classical bivalence while denying that every adjacent pair must share the same status.

concepts.card: Supervaluationism evaluates a vague statement across admissible ways of making its terms precise. A statement true under every such interpretation is supertrue; some borderline statements are neither supertrue nor superfalse. This permits truth-value gaps while preserving many classical logical laws, including excluded middle.

evidence.note: SEP section 3.3.1 defines admissible precisifications, supertruth and gaps while discussing retained classical laws; the card does not equate semantic indeterminacy with epistemic ignorance.

concepts.label: Supervaluationism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore evaluating a vague statement across admissible precise interpretations.

relations.note: The entry explicitly contrasts supervaluationism's semantic indeterminacy with epistemicism's unknown but sharp boundaries; this comparison explains their different treatments of borderline cases.

concepts.card: Indian Buddhist discussions of two truths distinguish conventional understanding from an ultimate perspective. Ordinary language and practices operate conventionally, while ultimate analysis asks how things really are. Buddhist schools interpret both levels and their relationship differently, so the distinction does not express one uniform doctrine across traditions.

evidence.note: SEP opening differentiates conventional and ultimate perspectives and explicitly warns that the schools can be radically opposed; the card avoids attributing one settled metaphysics or historical origin to all Buddhism.

concepts.label: Two truths in Indian Buddhist philosophy
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish conventional and ultimate truth while recognizing that Buddhist schools interpret the distinction differently.

relations.note: The distinction concerns perspectives on truth and knowledge, inviting comparison with epistemology's study of cognitive success without assimilating all Buddhist schools to a single Western theory.

concepts.card: Zhuangzi's butterfly dream reverses the security of waking identity: was Zhuangzi dreaming of a butterfly, or is a butterfly dreaming of Zhuangzi? In the cited interpretation, the story encourages modesty about one's present perspective. Feeling released from an earlier error need not establish a final standpoint.

evidence.note: SEP's discussion around Zhuangzi 2:14 links the story to perspectival shifts and mild skepticism; in the cited interpretation avoids claiming one uncontested reading or that the story proves reality illusory.

concepts.label: Zhuangzi’s butterfly dream
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine whether feeling awake guarantees a final, privileged perspective on experience.

relations.note: The dream provides a literary route into questions about certainty and cognitive perspective; this is an editorial learning bridge, not a claim that Zhuangzi adopted a modern epistemological doctrine.

concepts.card: Political science examines collective choices and conflicts, especially those involving government. A useful analysis asks which rules apply, what circumstances participants face and what choices they make. The same formal rule can produce different outcomes when the surrounding conditions or participants' strategies change.

evidence.note: OpenStax section 1.1 defines government-focused collective interactions and the rules/reality/choices framework; the final sentence expresses their interaction rather than a quantified causal finding.

imported_records.description: scientific study of politics
imported_records.subsection: Society and social sciences / Politics / Political science and the state

concepts.label: Political science
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine how rules and participants' choices shape collective decisions involving government.
concepts.original_description: scientific study of politics

relations.note: The chapter identifies a constitution as the most basic legal rules structuring government, one important instance of the rules its political-analysis framework examines.

concepts.card: A political constitution sets out basic principles governing public power, including institutional structure, governmental duties and people's rights. Those principles need not appear in a single document. Constitutional arrangements can combine written provisions with other sources, so a state's constitution is more than a document's title.

evidence.note: OpenStax section 1.1 identifies constitutional structure, duties and rights and gives multi-source examples; no claim that every constitutional guarantee is effectively enforced.

imported_records.description: set of fundamental principles or established precedents according to which a state or other organization is governed
imported_records.subsection: Society and social sciences / Law / Constitutional law

concepts.label: Constitution (politics)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how basic rules assign governmental powers, duties and limits.
concepts.original_description: set of fundamental principles or established precedents according to which a state or other organization is governed

relations.note: The passage explicitly distinguishes constitutional functions from having a single constitutional document, with the UK among its examples.

concepts.card: Parliamentary sovereignty is the UK's principle that Parliament is the supreme legal authority and can make or repeal laws. One Parliament cannot generally prevent a later Parliament from changing its legislation. Institutional reforms may constrain how power is exercised without, in this account, extinguishing that legal principle.

evidence.locator: Opening and Developments affecting Parliamentary sovereignty
evidence.note: UK Parliament's sovereignty page states supremacy, future repeal and reforms; generally and in this account preserve the official explanation's legal qualifications and avoid denying practical political constraints.

concepts.label: Parliamentary sovereignty
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore Parliament's legal supremacy in the UK and its relationship with institutional reforms.

relations.note: The official page presents sovereignty as a central principle of the UK's partly written, uncodified constitution, directly connecting principle and constitutional form.

concepts.card: An uncodified constitution lacks one consolidated constitutional text, not necessarily written rules. The United Kingdom's constitutional arrangements include many statutes alongside other sources. Calling the constitution unwritten can therefore mislead: the important distinction is whether its basic rules are collected in a single authoritative document.

evidence.locator: Parliamentary sovereignty and the UK constitution
evidence.note: UK Parliament's sovereignty page expressly describes the constitution as partly written and wholly uncodified; the card does not equate uncodified with informal, unenforceable or absent.

concepts.label: Uncodified constitution
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish lacking a single constitutional document from lacking written constitutional rules.

relations.note: The page identifies uncodified as the form of the UK's constitution, while explaining that many constitutional rules are nevertheless written in statutes.

concepts.card: The Parliament Act 1911 followed the Lords' rejection of the 1909 budget. It replaced their veto over most Commons public bills with delay, while excluding bills extending Parliament beyond five years. The 1949 Act shortened that delay, showing how legislative power shifted between the chambers.

evidence.locator: Why were the Parliament Acts brought into force?; Bills not subject to the Parliament Acts
evidence.note: UK Parliament history and Bills not subject sections support the 1909 conflict, qualified veto reduction, exclusion of extensions beyond five years and 1949 shortening. This is not a rule for every bill or all changes to parliamentary duration.

concepts.label: Parliament Act 1911
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect the 1909 budget conflict with replacing most Lords vetoes by delay.

relations.note: The official explanation sets the Act within normal Commons–Lords agreement and specifies circumstances where one chamber's consent can be bypassed.

concepts.card: The Salisbury convention restrains the House of Lords from voting down government bills promised in an election manifesto. It helps an elected government advance its announced program even without a Lords majority. This convention concerns how a chamber exercises its powers, rather than a new statutory voting procedure.

evidence.note: UK Parliament's Salisbury section states manifesto-bill restraint and lack of a Lords majority; describing it as a convention distinguishes the source's separate account of statutory Parliament Acts procedures.

concepts.label: Salisbury convention
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore restraint by the Lords toward government bills promised in an election manifesto.

relations.note: Compare a political convention limiting opposition to manifesto bills with a statutory route around Lords consent; both affect inter-chamber relations but operate through different mechanisms.

concepts.card: Under the UK Parliament Acts, a Speaker-certified money bill can reach Royal Assent without Lords consent after a month without unamended passage. It must already have passed the Commons and reached the Lords at least a month before session-end; the Commons can direct otherwise.

evidence.locator: Bills subject to the Parliament Acts
evidence.note: The Parliamentary Counsel guidance, paragraphs 1.2, 1.5, 1.8 and 2.2, supplies certification and all timing/direction conditions; this supersedes the introductory page's misleading claim of automatic assent within a month and its absolute amendment claim.

evidence.locator: Paragraphs 1.2, 1.5, 1.8 and 2.2; 2.7 and 2.19 resolve misleading simplifications
evidence.note: Official guidance supports certification, Commons passage, session timing, a month without unamended Lords passage, Commons contrary direction and Royal Assent; not automatic enactment after a month.

concepts.label: Money bills under the Parliament Acts
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare the Lords' restricted role over money bills with other public bills.

relations.note: The guidance expressly identifies section 1 of the 1911 Act as the money-bill procedure and reproduces its legal conditions.

concepts.card: Bicameralism organizes a legislature into two chambers. In the United Kingdom, the Commons and Lords normally both pass a bill before it becomes law, but the Parliament Acts create specified exceptions. The example shows that two chambers need not possess equal or unrestricted blocking powers.

evidence.locator: Opening and Bills subject to the Parliament Acts
evidence.note: UK Parliament's opening describes two-house agreement and exceptions; the card confines the mechanics to the UK and does not universalize its unequal powers across all bicameral systems.

concepts.label: Bicameralism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand two-chamber lawmaking through the qualified Commons–Lords example.

relations.note: The Parliament Acts page directly explains the two chambers' ordinary role through the statutory exceptions that modify it.

concepts.card: Mixed-member proportional representation combines constituency representatives with party-list seats intended to make overall representation proportional. In New Zealand's version, voters choose a local candidate and a party separately. The party vote largely determines each party's total seats, while electorate winners take individual constituency seats.

evidence.locator: Two votes; electorate MPs and list MPs
evidence.note: New Zealand Electoral Commission's MMP explanation supports separate votes and the overall party share; intended and largely accommodate allocation qualifications, and New Zealand's version prevents universalizing its exact rules.

concepts.label: Mixed-member proportional representation
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how constituency representation combines with a party-proportional seat total.

relations.note: The official MMP explanation identifies the threshold as the New Zealand eligibility rule operating within this electoral system, not as a universal property of MMP.

concepts.card: New Zealand's MMP system gives parties two routes to parliamentary eligibility: at least five percent of the party vote or an electorate victory. The alternative route means a party below the percentage threshold can still qualify through local success. These are New Zealand's rules, not universal MMP requirements.

evidence.locator: Political parties try to win party votes and electorate votes
evidence.note: The Electoral Commission explicitly states the five-percent or electorate-seat alternatives; the card does not claim an exact seat entitlement or apply the threshold to other countries.

concepts.label: New Zealand MMP threshold
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore two alternative routes to eligibility for proportional representation.

relations.note: The official page locates the threshold within New Zealand's MMP allocation and explains it alongside separate party and electorate votes.

concepts.card: A confidence and supply agreement allows one party to support another on specified parliamentary matters without forming a coalition government together. New Zealand's electoral authority distinguishes these arrangements from parties joining government. The distinction shows that keeping a government functioning need not mean sharing its entire program.

evidence.locator: Parties negotiate to form a government
evidence.note: The Electoral Commission's Parties negotiate section differentiates coalition membership from support on certain issues/laws; the card does not claim all agreements have identical terms or require support on every bill.

concepts.label: Confidence and supply agreement
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish supporting a government on specified matters from joining its coalition.

relations.note: The New Zealand MMP explanation discusses confidence and supply as one arrangement parties may negotiate when no party can govern alone, not an inevitable consequence of MMP.

concepts.card: Germany's constructive vote of no confidence requires the Bundestag to elect a successor Chancellor by a majority of its members while seeking the incumbent's dismissal. Opposition must therefore agree on a replacement, not merely on rejection. Article 67 also requires forty-eight hours between motion and election.

evidence.note: Basic Law Article 67 supplies majority membership, successor election, dismissal request and waiting period; the institutional consequence follows those express conditions and is bounded to Germany.

concepts.label: Constructive vote of no confidence
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why Germany requires choosing a successor while removing the Chancellor.

relations.note: Compare Germany's constitutional replacement requirement with New Zealand's negotiated support arrangements. Both concern parliamentary support for government, but one is a removal procedure and the other an interparty agreement.

concepts.card: Germany's eternity clause makes certain constitutional amendments inadmissible, including changes affecting the federal division into Länder and principles protected by Articles 1 and 20. This differs from merely requiring a large majority: Article 79 sets substantive limits that the ordinary two-thirds amendment procedure cannot override.

evidence.note: Basic Law Article 79(2)–(3) distinguishes two-thirds votes from inadmissible amendments; including avoids claiming that the examples exhaust the clause, and no universal claim about all constitutions is made.

concepts.label: German eternity clause
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a difficult amendment from a constitutionally inadmissible amendment.

relations.note: The clause exemplifies a constitutional limit on the power to amend basic governmental rules; the Basic Law provision and general constitution account support that editorial placement.

concepts.card: In Germany's concurrent legislative sphere, the Länder generally may legislate while the Federation has not exercised its power. Federal legislation can therefore change the space for state action. Article 72 also permits departures in specified fields, so concurrency does not mean either unrestricted coexistence or uniform federal exclusion.

evidence.note: Basic Law Articles 70–72, reinspected through all of Article 72, support the general rule and paragraph 3 exceptions; generally and specified fields avoid falsely absolute federal displacement.
The general federal-displacement rule has specified Land-departure exceptions; all of Article 72 was reinspected in source-raw/stage-b-german-competence.json.

concepts.label: Concurrent legislative powers in Germany
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how federal action can displace state legislative authority within a shared competence.

relations.note: Concurrent competence is a constitutional allocation of lawmaking authority between governmental levels, a specific example of the powers and structure a constitution defines.

concepts.card: In US federal court, standing ordinarily requires a concrete, particularized injury that is actual or imminent, linked to the challenged conduct and likely to be redressed by a favorable decision. Disagreeing with a policy is therefore different from showing the personal stake needed to bring the lawsuit.

evidence.note: Cornell's federal-standing section gives injury, causation and likely redressability; the jurisdiction is explicit and ordinarily avoids implying this short statement exhausts every standing doctrine.

concepts.label: Standing to sue
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a concrete, redressable legal injury from disagreement with government policy.

relations.note: Standing concerns a party's ability to bring suit; amicus participation lets a nonparty offer a brief under court rules. The comparison separates initiating litigation from contributing to its consideration.

concepts.card: In US court practice, an amicus curiae is a nonparty offering arguments or information through a brief. An interest in the case does not make the contributor a litigant. Each court's applicable rules govern when and how such outside submissions may be made.

evidence.note: Cornell defines the nonparty role and cites US Supreme Court Rule 37 and Federal Appellate Rule 29. US scope is explicit, while court-specific requirements avoid a universal permission or party-status claim.

concepts.label: Amicus curiae
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how a nonparty can contribute a brief to a court's consideration.

relations.note: Compare a nonparty's rule-governed contribution with the injury-based requirements for a plaintiff's federal standing. An amicus brief does not itself give its author party status.

concepts.card: In US criminal law, lenity favors the defendant when a statute remains ambiguous. It concerns interpreting a penal law's reach, rather than deciding whether evidence proves the conduct. Its rationale includes reserving the definition of crimes and punishments to lawmakers instead of judicial expansion.

evidence.note: Cornell's definition and separation-of-powers rationale support criminal-law ambiguity and legislative responsibility; remains ambiguous avoids suggesting every initial uncertainty immediately triggers the rule.

concepts.label: Rule of lenity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore construing unresolved criminal-law ambiguity in a defendant's favor.

relations.note: Lenity concerns ambiguity in a criminal law's meaning; the prosecution's burden concerns evidentiary proof of guilt. The sources support this distinction without treating them as interchangeable safeguards.

concepts.card: Habeas corpus brings the legality of custody before a court. In US federal practice, a detainee's petition is a civil action challenging detention rather than an ordinary new criminal trial. It can protect against unlawful confinement, but jurisdictional and procedural requirements limit when relief is available.

evidence.note: Cornell's overview and federal-procedure discussion support custody review, civil action and procedural limits; the card does not promise a merits hearing or release whenever a petition is filed.

concepts.label: Habeas corpus
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish judicial review of detention's lawfulness from an ordinary new criminal trial.

relations.note: Gideon's unsuccessful state habeas petition supplies a concrete example of challenging detention through habeas before later Supreme Court review; it does not establish that every habeas claim succeeds.

concepts.card: Stare decisis promotes consistency by directing courts to follow precedent. In the cited US account, vertical precedent comes from higher courts; horizontal precedent concerns a court's own earlier decisions. The Supreme Court can overrule its precedents, so continuity does not make every prior ruling permanent.

evidence.note: Cornell distinguishes horizontal and vertical precedent, cites the US Supreme Court’s limits on stare decisis and gives Brown as an example. The revised card does not imply lower courts may disregard binding higher-court precedent.

concepts.label: Stare decisis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare following a higher court with following one's own prior decisions.

relations.note: Cornell explicitly uses Brown's rejection of the separate-but-equal precedent as an example showing that stare decisis is not absolute.

concepts.card: The burden of proof concerns who must establish a proposition and what standard their evidence must meet. In US criminal cases, the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; most civil claims use preponderance of evidence. Different proceedings therefore demand different levels of evidentiary persuasion.

evidence.note: Cornell's criminal/civil examples, production/persuasion distinction and jurisdictional qualifications support the card; most civil claims preserves exceptions and the criminal claim is confined to proving guilt.

imported_records.description: in law, the obligation on a party in a trial to produce evidence
