imported_records.hook: Who must establish a claim, and what does that requirement mean?

concepts.label: Burden of proof
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare who must prove a proposition with how much proof the proceeding requires.
concepts.original_description: in law, the obligation on a party in a trial to produce evidence

relations.note: Compare the standard governing proof with a procedure asking whether a material factual dispute requires trial. Summary judgment does not simply replace evidentiary burdens with a judge's preference.

concepts.card: In US federal civil procedure, summary judgment can resolve a claim without trial when no genuine dispute of material fact remains and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. It does not authorize choosing between competing evidence that a reasonable factfinder could resolve differently.

evidence.note: Cornell's Rule 56 section and favorable-to-nonmovant discussion support both conditions and the factual-dispute limitation; the card is explicitly federal and civil rather than a universal rule for all courts.

concepts.label: Summary judgment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand deciding a claim without trial when no material factual dispute requires resolution.

relations.note: Both may be considered before trial, but summary judgment adjudicates a claim or issue while a preliminary injunction supplies interim protection before final judgment.

concepts.card: A preliminary injunction provides court-ordered protection before final judgment. In US federal practice, the cited test considers likely success, likely irreparable harm, competing hardships and the public interest. The question is whether interim relief is justified while the dispute remains unresolved, not whether the applicant has already won.

evidence.note: Cornell's Winter factors and Rule 65 discussion support the four considerations and interim role; federal qualification avoids treating varying state procedures as identical.

concepts.label: Preliminary injunction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore temporary relief before final judgment and why irreparable harm matters.

relations.note: Contrast temporary relief pending resolution with an adjudication without trial when material facts do not require a factfinder; the procedures answer different questions despite possible pretrial timing.

concepts.card: In US litigation, claim preclusion generally prevents repeating a cause of action after a final judgment on its merits. A losing plaintiff cannot simply sue the same defendant again on that claim; a winning plaintiff likewise cannot start another suit just to obtain additional recovery.

evidence.note: Cornell's res judicata overview and Bar and Merger examples support both losing and winning plaintiffs; generally avoids treating the brief account as an exhaustive jurisdiction-independent test.
The issue-specific definition supports the stated contrast with a repeated cause of action.

concepts.label: Claim preclusion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why a resolved cause of action generally cannot be litigated again.

relations.note: The res judicata entry expressly distinguishes claim preclusion from issue preclusion; the former concerns the cause of action, while the latter concerns a decided issue.

concepts.card: In US litigation, issue preclusion can bar relitigation of an issue actually litigated and necessarily decided in a valid final judgment. It generally binds a party who had a full and fair opportunity to litigate, with recognized nonparty exceptions. The issue may recur within a different claim.

evidence.note: The original collateral-estoppel entry supports the factual/legal issue and final-necessary-determination core. Its concise definition does not alone supply the full applicability boundary; the explicit Cornell issue-preclusion entry and Taylor opinion supply those conditions.
The claim-level definition supports the stated contrast with a previously decided issue.

evidence.locator: Opening; elements 1–4; contrast with claim preclusion; nonparty paragraph (lines 5–16)
evidence.note: Requires the identical issue to have been actually litigated and determined, essential to a valid final judgment. A different later cause of action can still involve that issue. The nonparty discussion is read alongside the primary opinion, not as an absolute same-parties rule.

The Court describes actual litigation and necessary resolution, full and fair opportunity, the general rule against binding nonparties, and limited recognized exceptions. Supports can bar and generally binds without requiring identical parties in every later suit.

concepts.label: Issue preclusion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish relitigating a decided issue from repeating an entire claim.

relations.note: The linked accounts distinguish preventing a repeated claim from preventing a repeated decision on an essential issue, while acknowledging varied uses of the term res judicata.

concepts.card: Citizens' assemblies bring selected members of the public together to learn, hear contrasting evidence and deliberate on a policy question. In Ireland's process, participants discuss in small groups and make recommendations. Those recommendations are advisory: elected institutions retain responsibility for deciding legislation and government policy.

evidence.locator: How does the Citizens' Assembly work?; recommendations
evidence.note: Ireland's official FAQ supports evidence, facilitated discussion and advisory recommendations; the card explicitly bounds decision authority to the Irish process rather than every citizens' assembly internationally.

imported_records.description: Bringing selected members of the public together to examine policy questions.

concepts.label: Citizens' assemblies
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore informed public deliberation whose recommendations remain advisory in Ireland.
concepts.original_description: Bringing selected members of the public together to examine policy questions.

relations.note: The FAQ directly explains stratified random recruitment as the method for forming an Irish assembly intended to broadly reflect the wider population.

concepts.card: Ireland's citizens' assembly recruitment combines chance with demographic balancing. Randomly invited households may nominate an adult applicant; members are then selected using demographic information so the group broadly resembles society. The resulting mini-public is intended to be diverse, rather than simply comprising whoever volunteers first.

evidence.locator: How are members selected?; recruitment method
evidence.note: The official FAQ's recruitment paragraphs describe random household invitations, one adult nominee and stratified selection among applicants; intended and broadly avoid claiming perfect representativeness or eliminating nonresponse effects.

concepts.label: Stratified sortition for citizens’ assemblies
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how lottery recruitment and demographic stratification produce an intended mini-public.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies stratified selection as the membership-recruitment procedure for Irish citizens' assemblies, connecting mechanism and deliberative body.

concepts.card: A regulatory sandbox permits supervised testing of an innovation within defined limits. The UK's Financial Conduct Authority typically uses small, time-limited trials with real consumers. Acceptance does not remove authorization requirements or exempt a firm from national law, distinguishing controlled experimentation from unrestricted permission to operate.

evidence.locator: What the Regulatory Sandbox offers; tests; tools
evidence.note: FCA sections on offers, tests and tools support real consumers, scale/duration limits, authorization and inability to waive national law; the specific mechanics remain attributed to this regulator's program.

concepts.label: Regulatory sandbox
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish supervised, limited testing from exemption from regulation.

relations.note: Compare time-limited regulatory testing with automatic statutory expiry: both impose a time boundary, but a sandbox limits a trial while a sunset provision ends legal authority unless renewed.

concepts.card: The US Freedom of Information Act lets people request existing federal agency records, subject to specified exemptions. It does not require an agency to create new records, conduct research or answer a questionnaire. The right therefore concerns access to recorded information rather than a general government research service.

evidence.locator: What is the FOIA?; What can I ask for?
evidence.note: FOIA.gov's definition and What can I ask for? support agency-record scope, exemptions and no new-research obligation; people avoids incorrectly limiting requesters to US citizens.

concepts.label: Freedom of Information Act (United States)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand access to existing federal agency records subject to specified exemptions.

relations.note: FOIA concerns access to agency records; the Sunshine Act concerns observation of covered agency meetings. Their comparison distinguishes two transparency mechanisms with different scopes and exceptions.

concepts.card: FOIA segregability means an exempt passage does not necessarily justify withholding an entire record. Federal agencies must consider partial disclosure and release reasonably separable nonexempt portions after redaction. The practical question is what can still be disclosed without revealing the information protected by a valid exemption.

evidence.note: 5 USC 552(a)(8)(A)(ii) and the final paragraph of (b) require reasonable segregation and partial release; reasonably and valid exemption preserve limits rather than promising every document has releasable fragments.

concepts.label: FOIA segregability
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why an exempt passage need not justify withholding the entire record.

relations.note: The statute itself imposes partial-disclosure and segregation duties within FOIA, tying the mechanism directly to the federal records-access regime.

concepts.card: The Government in the Sunshine Act generally opens meetings of covered federal collegial agencies to public observation. Its definition does not cover every government gathering. Specified exceptions permit closure of portions, with formal voting and disclosure procedures, so openness is a structured legal requirement rather than an unlimited rule.

evidence.note: 5 USC 552b(a)–(d) defines covered collegial agencies, public observation, exceptions and recorded votes; covered and portions avoid universalizing coverage or suggesting every discussion must be public.

concepts.label: Government in the Sunshine Act
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore public observation of covered federal agency meetings and formal closure procedures.

relations.note: Meeting observation under section 552b and access to records under FOIA address different forms of government transparency; neither mechanism is treated as an automatic substitute for the other.

concepts.card: A sunset provision makes a law, program or agency expire after a specified period unless renewed through the required legislative process. Instead of requiring a fresh decision to terminate it, the provision makes continuation depend on renewed approval. This changes the default when lawmakers take no action.

evidence.note: Cornell's sunset-law definition and two-year program example support automatic expiry and renewal; required legislative process avoids assuming every sunset uses identical review procedures.

concepts.label: Sunset provision
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand automatic expiration as a way to require renewed legislative approval.

relations.note: A sunset changes the default duration of legal authority; a sandbox bounds a supervised test. Their shared time limit is useful to compare without equating the institutional mechanisms.

concepts.card: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission addressed abuses associated with apartheid through separate work on human-rights violations, reparations and rehabilitation, and amnesty. Its committee structure shows that truth-finding, assistance to victims and decisions about perpetrators' amnesty were related tasks, rather than one undifferentiated act of forgiveness.

evidence.note: The official TRC introduction identifies the post-apartheid mandate and three committees; the card describes institutional tasks rather than claiming universal reconciliation or automatic forgiveness.

concepts.label: South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare truth-finding, reparations and amnesty as separate parts of a post-apartheid process.

relations.note: The official site identifies the Amnesty Committee as one of the Commission's three components, directly locating amnesty decisions within its wider mandate.

concepts.card: Amnesty before South Africa's TRC was conditional, not automatic for politically connected violence. In a 1997 decision, Henry Khanyile's application failed because the committee found he had withheld relevant facts. The case shows why political context did not remove the requirement for full disclosure.

evidence.locator: 18 August 1997 statement; Khanyile and Tumahole decisions
evidence.note: The TRC's 18 August 1997 statement quotes the committee's section 20(1)(c) nondisclosure finding; the card reports its decision without asserting that disclosure alone guaranteed amnesty or retrying guilt independently.

concepts.label: Conditional amnesty in South Africa's TRC
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why political context alone did not guarantee amnesty without full disclosure.

relations.note: The statement is an actual Amnesty Committee decision within the TRC process and expressly applies its statutory full-disclosure condition.

concepts.card: Brown v. Board of Education rejected state-imposed racial segregation in US public education under equal protection. The Court treated separate schooling as inherently unequal, rather than asking only whether physical facilities matched. The decision challenged a legal framework of separation, although implementing desegregation required further proceedings and resistance persisted.

evidence.locator: Brown v. Board of Education case summary
evidence.note: The US Courts educational account supports the public-education holding and later compliance/resistance discussion; state-imposed and public preserve constitutional scope without claiming immediate practical integration or a rule covering every private activity.

concepts.label: Brown v. Board of Education
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore the constitutional rejection of state-mandated racial segregation in public education.

relations.note: Brown illustrates the possibility of departing from precedent: Cornell's stare decisis entry expressly connects it with rejection of Plessy's separate-but-equal rule, while the court account supplies the education holding.

concepts.card: Gideon v. Wainwright established the right to appointed counsel for indigent defendants in state felony trials. After Gideon was denied a lawyer, the Supreme Court held that the Sixth Amendment guarantee applies to states through the Fourteenth Amendment. The case concerns fair criminal proceedings, not universal publicly funded legal representation.

evidence.note: US Courts Facts and Reasoning support Florida felony prosecution, indigence, denial and incorporation; the card confines its claim to state felony trials rather than all civil disputes or every minor offense.

concepts.label: Gideon v. Wainwright
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect an indigent defendant's denied lawyer with the right to appointed counsel in state felony trials.

relations.note: The case summary explicitly records Gideon's state habeas petition challenging his detention after the denial of counsel, before his later Supreme Court petition.
